“In any truly advanced civilization that gets depicted [in science fiction], you really see two pillars of scientific progress. One is some form of AGI, and the other a simulation. And I was always more drawn to the idea of simulation.” – Joon Sung Park, Co-Founder and CEO of Simile

Before Joon Sung Park and I had ever met, he simulated the conversation. What questions would Mario, or a person like Mario, ask him? What would I find most interesting to dig into? I do not know how closely I adhered to my facsimile, though I wish I did.

Joon has an advantage in rehearsing these encounters, and thousands of others. He is the Co-founder and CEO of Simile, an applied AI company building a foundation model of human behavior. That involves creating digital twins of real people – like a writer or podcaster – and simulating how they might react to certain circumstances. As you might imagine, that’s an attractive proposition for many companies: CVS Health, for instance, can test a new pricing policy against thousands of simulated patients. A bank can model how customers will react before announcing a fee change. Joon’s ambitions stretch far beyond these cases, though, and Simile has raised more than $300 million, most recently at a $2 billion valuation, to pursue them.

The portrait artist always paints themselves. I loved this line from Joon, who happens to be a gifted painter in his own right. When apprehending a piece of art – whatever the medium – I can sometimes forget to consider what it tells us about the author rather than the subject.

“Emotional rigor.” Another phrase of Joon’s that I’ve been sitting with. This was how he described the intensity one needs to build to paint a beautiful painting of someone. You need to build this deep, rigorous connection. This is a universal lesson, I think, and especially true in writing.

Contradictory superpowers. Another really sharp heuristic (can you tell I enjoyed this conversation quite a lot?). When it comes to hiring, this is what Joon looks for: someone with two strengths that rarely go together. For example, a colleague with deep scientific seriousness and a very playful side.

Working backwards. Joon’s ultimate goal is not to give Simile a question and have it make a prediction. It is to give a “wicked” problem like climate change and have it simulate a superabundance of possible paths to help us find the best one.

Who wins when everything is predictable? If simulation becomes as ubiquitous as Simile suggests it might, how do companies compete with one another? Is “strategy,” as a broad discipline, solved? Joon pointed to a few thoughts on where edge might still live – namely in point of view, proprietary data, and compute. Now, this is just a thought experiment, of course. But two of those three presumably redound to the world’s best-resourced companies, which is far from ideal.

When I asked Joon what book he'd assign to everyone, he named The Catcher in the Rye, which he first read at around 14 or 15. He was careful to say that the books that matter most are deeply personal, but Holden Caulfield's visceral portrait of a young mind stuck with him. Earlier in our conversation, he also pointed to Asimov's Foundation series as a core inspiration for Simile, and particularly the idea of psychohistory: giving a simulator a desired end state and working backwards to find the path there.

Jon Ronson has a new book out, The Castle. I’m only a few pages in, but given that I’ve loved all of his other bizarre, freewheeling investigations, I suspect I’ll like it quite a bit.

Grok Bot is really very good at this point. I suspect this form factor – persistent, proactive, task-specific bots overseen by an orchestrator – will become the default for professional work. It’s the closest thing to having a collection of digital coworkers.

Mario Gabriele: If you can predict the future, then you could be the world’s greatest hedge fund ever.

Joon Sung Park: So it’s a really interesting question. Simile is an applied AI layer that basically allows you to predict people’s behavior at the level of individuals and populations. We can predict people’s behavior with 85% plus accuracy.

Mario Gabriele: And the ultimate goal is to simulate all 8 billion humans and predict the future in some sense?

Joon Sung Park: Yes, it is about representing people in our society and also try to understand the interaction between them. A lot of the companies that we work with, they want to talk to their niche population all the time, but they can maybe, if they’re lucky, to get to talk to them once, but we create simulations of them once, then they can ask them any questions.

So this is actually the strength for a simulation. So the problems that we want to go after is really ask questions like, well, how to solve climate change? Can we actually find out the signals for democracy that’s about to collapse? So this is what social scientists would call wicked problems. I often, before interviews, simulate how the interview might go.

What are some of the interesting questions that you might ask me today?

Mario Gabriele: A pharmacy chain wants to know why its patients stop taking their pills. A bank is about to change what it charges. A CEO is preparing to walk into an earnings call. None of them know what will happen. But Joon Sung Park just might. Joon is the co-founder and CEO of Simile. In 2023, as a Stanford PhD student, he published a paper that put 25 AI agents in a small virtual town and watched them throw a Valentine’s party.

Simile is that idea grown up: digital twins of real people, built from hours of interviews that let companies like CVS test a decision on thousands of simulated customers before making a real one. That pitch has helped Simile raise more than $300 million and reach a $2 billion valuation. In this episode, we discuss Joon’s past as a painter, why the end market for a simulation company might be a hedge fund, and what happens to strategy once everyone can see the future.

Joon, I’ve been super excited about this conversation because I think you’re building one of the most interesting companies I’ve ever imagined. Uh, so maybe we can just start very simply. Tell us about Simile.

Joon Sung Park: So Simile is an applied AI layer that is creating a foundation model of human behavior that basically allows you to predict people’s behavior at the level of individuals and populations. We then have an amazing product team, an engineering team that takes the core foundation model into a product that allows our users to ask any questions they might have, whether it’s their customers at large, institutions or their environment, and so forth.

Mario Gabriele: The implication of, of Simile is in a sense that humans are extremely predictable, right? I’m interested in, in whether you find that to be true in your own life. Do you find that the people you know actually surprise you a lot of the time, or are actually, you think you could simulate them extremely well?

Joon Sung Park: What I do think is the case is I do think we can learn about people. What we’ve noticed over time is that people are made of fundamental building blocks. The core nature that they contain seem to be fairly consistent, so we can learn about them. So, for instance, if I have a close friend that I’ve known since high school, I know what kind of food he likes, but I also know what excites him or what makes him sad.

These are the fundamental natures. So one of the core theses is at the level of individuals, we can pay attention to these kinds of signals that people might have and learn about what would excite them, what is the meaning they seek, and so forth. Now, an exciting part is when you bring in many of these people together in a room, then you then see an amazing emergent phenomenon as well.

And that’s actually much harder to predict in some ways. But this is also what gives us the ability to explore different causal mechanisms. So had we done this, if we had this policy, will that change the world in certain ways? Those are the kind of exploration that we would want to do in simulations.

Mario Gabriele: When you talk about emergent phenomenon, what does that look like when you start to bring these people together?

Joon Sung Park: Emergence actually goes back all the way to complex systems and perhaps even the early days of simulation research. So in many ways, the simulation that we’re creating with generative AI models is a revived form of the research that had gone in for many decades. But if you look back to 1970s, one of the scholars that I respect the most is Thomas Schelling.

He was a behavioral economist who created really the field around what we called agent-based models. And he was really one of the first simulation researchers in computation. The model that he became known for was—of course, simulation of the era really cares deeply about the societal problems of the era, and 1970s, it was the racial segregation.

The model he created was the model of—a model of segregation that basically made this point. Imagine for a moment that you have a checkerboard. On this checkerboard, there are red dots and blue dots. These are quote-unquote agents in the system. Now, these agents, because it was back in 1970s, were extremely simple in the primitives.

They had one rule: every game iteration, they would look around their corner and see how many of its neighbors are of the same color. If the ratio drops below a certain point, then that agent would decide to move to a random location. The point that Thomas Schelling was trying to make was, in our society, we believe that racial segregation happens due to overt racism that people held within them, but that’s actually not the case.

People can have very subtle preference towards living with people of the same color. So in no way extreme or overt, but that simple motion would still be enough to generate complete segregation of the society. So that’s an instance of emergent phenomenon. Yes. Where if you look at any individuals within the society, you would not imagine these people to be racist.

However, the societies trend towards being segregated. That was an unexpected finding. Now, of course, that was early days of simulation research. Thomas Schelling goes on to win a Nobel Prize. But now the opportunity that we see is can we create simulation that is of much higher fidelity than what Thomas Schelling used to do?

So, of course, 1970s we had the limitation in models—these were deterministic models. But now that we have generative AI model that actually encodes a lot of human behaviors, instead of saying red dots and blue dots with these simple rules, can we actually put them in a much more realistic environment?

So the kind of problems that we would want to go after in the most ambitious side of the scientific research is really ask questions like, well, tell me how to solve climate change. Climate change is a really interesting problem because it has so many actors with competing incentives. So this is what social scientists would call wicked problems.

Joon Sung Park: Can we actually find out the signals for democracy that’s about to collapse? It’s these kind of problems that we would be investigating with the next generation of simulation technology.

Mario Gabriele: Mhm. When did you first become acquainted with Schelling and simulation work? Like when did you fall down that rabbit hole?

Joon Sung Park: So I actually grew up as a big science fiction fan. As you know, growing up, I watched, read a lot of science fiction, and one of the core things I always resonated with was this idea that in any truly advanced civilization that gets depicted, you really see two pillars of scientific progress. One is some form of AGI and the other a simulation.

And I always thought that was super fascinating. And for whatever reason, I was always more drawn to this idea of simulation.

Joon Sung Park: And I also think a little bit more uh, philosophically speaking, so I initially got my training as a painter. Yes. In, in art.

Joon Sung Park: And I think it was perhaps a little bit related to that passion as well. But simulation, when done right, it’s a little bit like painting a portrait of the society.

Joon Sung Park: So that we can learn about the society and so forth. So I always had a lot of interest in the topic of simulation. But then during college years, I got acquainted with the topic around agent-based models. And so that’s when I initially started to learn about this topic and did a very brief stint as an RA in a lab that tried to go deeper into the agent-based model field.

And then I sort of forgot about it for a good number of years. And when I started my PhD at Stanford—so this was 2020 and GPT-3 was just about to come out, and there was a lot of chatters around the scientific field that this new class of model is going to be a powerful new mechanism for understanding people and also for AI.

So during that first year, myself and two of my co-founders, Michael Bernstein and Percy Liang, wrote a paper called On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models. So this was in particular project that Percy led at Stanford that coined the term foundation model. But as we were working on this project, we started to really think about, well, imagine for a moment the foundation model and these generative AI models will be an important part of our technological landscape. What’s going to be the killer application of the technology? Yeah, and we realized that it might be simulation, because these models have ingested so much of human behavioral data that we noticed that if you poke at models at the right angle, we can actually extract a lot of human behavior, in which case this can actually be the fundamental building block that we had missed in the past for building simulation. So that when we had that realization, I sort of connected that with the agent-based models that I used to be fascinated by and said, can we create the next version, the next generation of agent-based models, and maybe even call it generative agent-based models?

And that really became some of the starting point for thinking about this topic and area.

Mario Gabriele: You mentioned the inspiration from sci-fi when I, you know, was studying Simile, the sort of direct comparison for me feels like psychohistory and Asimov. What were the inspirations for you when you think about what you were reading as a kid or you know that you reflect on now? Yeah.

Joon Sung Park: So Foundation series is actually a fantastic example here. What really inspires me from the science fiction is not only the existence of this kind of technology, but also the shape of this technology. So if you look at simulation technology today, at least the initial building blocks are basically technology that allows you to simulate the results of studies or policies.

Yes. So imagine that we have a behavior study that we want to run, market research we want to run. These are some initial sort of good use cases that people start with on day one. They would come in with a question. But what is interesting is the arc of this technology is much more proactive. And I can describe what that means from the lens of Isaac Asimov.

So if you look at the Foundation series, here’s a premise for, for those who may not be familiar with this story. So there’s a galactic empire. So it’s a, you know, much more into the future than where we are right now. And a group of scientists realize that this galactic empire is going to collapse in 1,000 years, and they are basically tasked with figuring out what is the way to reduce the following unrest after the collapse of this empire.

And they realized that there was going to be 30,000 years of unrest. And they asked, how can we reduce it to 1,000 years? So they asked their simulator, basically this question.

Joon Sung Park: What is the best way for us to ensure that the social unrest is kept at a thousand years? And if you look at this shape of this technology, the psychohistory, the simulator that they’re thinking about, what they’re giving this tool is an end state. They’re not giving them a question. They’re giving them a goal.

Here is the end state that we want to get to. Yes, it’s up to the simulator to create a multiverse of possibility and basically suggest maybe this one—and maybe using the term from Dune—the Golden Path for getting to that particular end outcome. This is the beauty of simulation, because this is possible for a simulation, because we care deeply about multiverse, creating these different possibilities, exploring into the future and also understanding the causal mechanism.

And, you know, the set for it becomes sort of increasingly grand. You know, his ambitions grow anyway. It’s another one that’s sort of in that rough zone. That is very interesting when I think about the sort of second, third X number of acts for this company. You can let your imagination spin almost infinitely.

One of them that I could imagine is, you know, I in my early years, I wanted to be a lawyer, and I did a lot of public speaking and mock trial. I imagine jury selection, for example, would be something that is like extremely applicable here. Have you started to see that?

Joon Sung Park: We have, um, in the legal spaces, policy spaces. I think the role the simulation can play is actually quite deep. So this is something that we are obviously quite inspired by. Um, and we do see that opportunity.

Mario Gabriele: Uh, what about in the personal space? Because when I think about the most impactful decisions in your life, picking a partner is one of them. Uh, is there, is there a world in which Simile becomes sufficiently well, you know, widely spread that people start to simulate potential matches?

Joon Sung Park: So I think it’s possible. And now what is interesting about this technology is simulation is one of those very few technologies that’s very applicable for any groups of people. So right now of course, we are partnering with enterprises to bring simulation, this innovation, to their organizations. But this is something that individuals can also leverage.

The use cases they might see are everywhere from, “Or, what is the better way for me to, let’s say, get better at public speaking?” And that’s a common use case that I have seen. Imagine you have a very difficult conversation that you need to have with your friend or with your colleagues. Is there a way to rehearse the situation so that you’re prepared for those conversations?

So I think these are the places that, that simulation could be leveraged. Of course, for the more, uh, sort of these dating and romantic side of things, I think this is an obvious use cases that some people might be interested in. And obviously I personally happen to be a little bit more of a romantic in some ways, where I let certain parts of my life just fall naturally.

So I think it does depend a little bit on who you are.

Mario Gabriele: You know, I don’t know if you’ve ever come across it, but there’s, I think, a—I mean, it’s the New York Times that has something called like the 21 Questions That Lead to Love. And there are these very good questions that are really thoughtful and do create a way for people to open up. I could imagine someone doing a vast survey of people of those 21 questions and using, you know, that to simulate something pretty interesting.

Obviously, that does not feel particularly on strategy for you to do, but it’s interesting that the technology is getting to the point where, yeah, you could, you could imagine something happening there.

Mario Gabriele: One of your earlier projects was called SimReddit, which I thought was really interesting.

Maybe you can actually talk a little bit about that.

Joon Sung Park: So this actually was the project that was the precursor to all the simulation effort and also a joint effort that we made at Stanford. So this actually predates the, the small Smallville Generative Agents paper. The idea was this. We worked on this back in 2021. The idea was, again, the models have seen so much of human behavior data that we can actually use these models to simulate people. We wanted to demonstrate that this actually had really good use cases.

The interesting part was we actually thought about creating generative agents in Smallville back in 2021, but we couldn’t convince ourselves that this was going to be useful. We were like, well, this is interesting, but is it a game? Like, why would we want to do this?

So we wanted to demonstrate a use case that we were compelled by. And one of the fields that I intersected with was this field called social computing. Social computing is a field that basically has to do with creating computational tools and platforms that enables people to interact with each other and collaborate with each other in a better and pro-social way.

And one of the hardest problems in this field for many decades has been the problem around emergence and cold start. So it’s one thing for you to run user study and see how five people might use your study, your platform. But what happens when you have millions of people using your platform? Whereas something that we hear often and all the time in many ways, is you design the new social networking service or you created a new online thread.

It’s very hard to tell what people will do in that space, all the ways they might misbehave, all the ways where they might find opportunities to collaborate. It’s really hard to foresee. This is where our policies would also fail. So if you look at Reddit, uh, each subreddit has these moderation strategies.

But oftentimes those are set as—in a react—in a reactive way to something that has happened. Our idea was, what if we can create a simulation of subreddits on day one, show the designers and users every single thing that could happen in this community so that we can—before we put people into this platform—we can put in the strategies and moderation tools and rules, and they will prevent some of the bad actors while encouraging some of the really good use cases.

So it was 2021–2022 version of book. That’s basically what this was.

Mario Gabriele: Yes, that’s right. I wouldn’t have made that connection to that. Totally makes sense. One of the things that was interesting to me about that is you were sort of simulating the fail states of a company, right? How much of that do you bring into Simile itself, like, have you simulated, I don’t know, your, your entire company and thought through, I don’t know, if XYZ things happen, we should be extra aware of them, right?

Joon Sung Park: So we do actually use Simile to make our own decisions. Obviously we want to believe that this is actually our core advantage as a company.

Joon Sung Park: So recently we had to decide whether we wanted to move our headquarters. So because we were coming out of Stanford, our first headquarters actually was in Palo Alto, and we asked the simulation where should we actually have our headquarters? Should it be in San Francisco or can we have it in South Bay? It was very compelling that, uh, yes, we actually would need to, uh, want to move our headquarters to San Francisco based on the simulation.

And this had to do with our ability to attract amazing colleagues that we want to work with, our ability to be in close proximity to some of our customers, and it has some downstream implications if we stayed in South Bay. So we decided, at least for Simile, it made sense to move.

Joon Sung Park: These are the kind of simulations that we would actually run.

Mario Gabriele: And so for, for that simulation is the sort of input population, current employees, potential employees and customers? Like how do you sort of make sure you have, you know, the stakeholders you need in that?

Joon Sung Park: The input to this particular simulation actually was initially, um, people working in tech in the Bay Area. And of course, that does naturally include people who might already be at this company, but that was the population that we tested against.

Mario Gabriele: What have been the predictions that have surprised you the most?

Joon Sung Park: We actually ran a study and that was trying to understand how automobile companies are to think about EV, the electric vehicles. This actually was a study that we ran for, for some time, even before we started Simile. But one of the problems they were faced with was how do we market electric vehicle?

And, you know, for companies that are not electric vehicle company. Yes, marketers and market researchers, what they were focused on was, well, what is the right messaging that would actually maximize the sales of EV? And we run that in simulation and we say, hey, you can say XYZ things and this is how your sales will change.

Reasonable. But what was surprising, however, was some of the best messages that you could create actually would change people’s perception across other lines of business that this set of companies had. That’s not EV.

Joon Sung Park: And what was interesting was it would actually lower the sales of other product lines that weren’t EV. So even though this particular strategy increased the performance on the EV sales, if you take a look at the holistic picture of the business, it was actually in the negative. That actually was really interesting, right?

To the point of us finding insight that’s counterintuitive here. Basically counterintuitive thing was you were tasked with optimizing for this micro, uh, sort of a segment of the business, but it actually can have negative implications across the board. So maybe it is actually not the right move. Of course, this is something the companies would want to take into consideration holistically and make their own decision.

Mario Gabriele: You must have a very good simulation of yourself in a sense. Do you try and increase the fidelity bit by bit over time? Does that happen naturally? Are you sort of—I could imagine a version of it where you’re like, I don’t know. Once a week I give a 30-minute call to my, my simulation in a sense, and let it, yeah, increase its, its fidelity.

Joon Sung Park: So what’s interesting is what we have—and this is an internal tool and not a part of our product yet—but internally on Slack channels for the company, we actually have what we call siblings. Siblings can actually model our own team members based on all the messaging that we’ve been having in the public channels and so forth.

So you can actually @ your sibling and ask it to talk to another siblings, ask it to talk back. And it’s actually a very good representation of that person. Yeah, we—and one of my team members actually made this more as a sort of a fun sort of hackathon project. Yes, but it actually became one of the more viral feature internally.

So, for instance, when teammates want to, you know, grab dinner, when they’re deciding what to eat, they would actually do, @ a group of siblings: “Decide what we want to eat.” Or if we have a debate that we want to sort of actually resolve, we’ve actually @ a bunch of siblings and say, hey, what would these group of people actually talk about?

Just simulate the entire debate in a multi-agent fashion. It has been, it has been quite fun.

Mario Gabriele: Wow, that’s so interesting. In many ways it feels like the, the final state business model of a company like yours should be investing. If you can predict the future, then you, you could be the world’s greatest hedge fund ever. Yeah. What do you think about that? How far away might that be?

Joon Sung Park: Simile, of course, was founded on the premise that we want to help people and society make the best decisions possible. And that is my personal passion. Um, so beyond obviously the monetary side of the business, um, you know, we were fundamentally researchers to start. So we do care deeply about the impact that we want to have, but the finance market is actually interesting, less even for the profit.

But actually because this is the way that our society decides to allocate capital for societal decision making. So I agree that this is actually the final one of the final landing spot, potentially for technology like Simile. We do have colleagues we hired directly from leading quant firms. And so this is of course something that we are quite fascinated by.

Mario Gabriele: Have you allowed it to trade small amounts yet?

Joon Sung Park: Not yet. Um, but I do think it might be an interesting exploration for, for Simile. We’re not going to be able to disclose it when it does happen, at least for some time. But it’s an interesting exploration.

Mario Gabriele: Yeah. You know, I think people have obviously let various agents loose on trading accounts, and it always seems like it goes rather badly so far. But this might be—I could imagine there being a real edge there.

Joon Sung Park: But the thing that I, that I do think this does raise that’s quite interesting is more and more agents in the future will be making decisions, and this will be the case in the financial market. This will also be the case when you’re trying to even create new UI and UX. Agents will be doing this, and they are already doing this.

Where they fail is when they do not take into consideration human nature of the world they operate in. Simulation is actually a way to inject our voice into this decision-making to basically give a sense to these AI models what people might actually do and feel, so that we can have also a better control over these models.

So that I actually do think is a very important part of contribution that the field of simulation has to make.

Mario Gabriele: It sort of raises an interesting conundrum that I’ve been trying to think of what it means. I’d be curious how you parse it in a world in which Simile or, you know, other such tools, let’s say, become truly table stakes for every company and kind of every significant organization. You’re then in a world in which every company has superior strategy, right?

How does someone win in that world? Is it just a sheer research—resource overmatch? Is it the rare moments of human intuition being somehow a little bit actually better than the simulation that make the difference? Because when we think about our world of startups, like strategy is, is kind of one of the key inputs to how a small company surpasses a big one.

Joon Sung Park: Eventually, I think there is basically three different elements here. One is it will always be humans who ask the goal and who ask the right questions. So a part of human intuition that is going to be—that will continue to be important here, is basically that ability to put things into the right framing that I do think will always be there.

Then I think there is a question around resources. And the resources I think come from two different axes. One is—and Simile does support this today—but this is the ability for these companies to create a simulator that is particularly fine-tuned for their population and their environment. A part of this will certainly be these companies bringing in their own data to create a forked version of Simile’s model that is going to be institutional, that will be used for their particular institution.

The last piece here is also compute. So with Simile you can create more multiverse. You can create more experiments. You can look into the future for a longer period of time. And where I actually do see this go is simulation is interesting as AI technology in the way that this is the most extreme version of inference-time compute, of reasoning.

This is the deepest reasoning a model can possibly do because we’re literally exploring every possibilities. We’re simulating what might happen. And another thing that is beautiful in this particular context is there’s actually no limit to how much you can simulate. So you can actually see—imagine you want to create a simulation that would solve climate change.

I’m sure that’s not going to be a $10 session of inference.

Joon Sung Park: So there I do actually think that differentiation might actually also come purely from the amount of compute and resources that we might have.

Mario Gabriele: I’d be curious to hear how you think about building your team and what you look for in researchers. That’s something that some folks I talked to before this said, you know, you have a particular lens of, of what works for you at Simile.

Joon Sung Park: What I always care about is very consistently two things: are they the common denominator of success? And do they have two superpowers that contradict each other? And these two things are something that, for me, at least for the people that I loved and respected the most and that they had most consistently.

The former is interesting because it allows us to see whether this is somebody who has extremely high degree of ownership. People who basically wake up in the morning and think, doesn’t matter how everything else goes. I would personally make sure that this succeed, that I can be the one to control the success of this particular project or this particular era.

Very powerful. But it also shows that they can reinvent themselves. This is something I personally cared a lot about and for myself for Simile and the team members, I want Simile to be relevant not just in the first era of our company, the era that we live in today. But I want us to be invited to play the next game and the game after and be relevant for many generations to come.

That does require us to be able to reinvent ourselves multiple times. And right now we are in the early innings of this journey, so we are now trying to gain the right to win this era and gain access to the next era. But I want the individual team members to also bring in that energy. The winning now doesn’t mean our journey is done.

It means we merely gain the right to play the next game, and it’s actually the ability to play the game that is the greatest prize. So that I actually care deeply about. Another one here is people with contradicting superpowers. I have now multiple people and in this who share this trait. But for instance, if you look at someone like Michael, who is one of my co-founders, he actually was the person that I brought and who I had started to discuss the idea of creating a game town.

And many of my senior-most colleagues thought that was silly, and these were colleagues that I loved and respected the most. But they thought, well, why are we making a game? Is this for entertainment? And I honestly didn’t quite have a good answer. And I was like, well, I think it might be just really interesting, but I actually don’t know.

But Michael was somebody who had this deep analytical insight. So he’s an extremely mature scientist, among the very best in my field, if not the best that we’ve seen. But he’s also internally a child. When he heard this idea and we sort of talk about it, you sort of would see his eyes light up. And he also couldn’t articulate why this was a good idea, but he knew that this was something that he wanted to do.

Being able to marry that childlike playfulness and imagination and boldness with the very deep, mature scientific expertise makes this character very compelling. So that I actually care deeply about. So I see this across my team members, and I feel very fortunate to be able to say that. But this is something that I do care about quite a bit.

Mario Gabriele: The loss of playfulness feels like the death of your mind in many ways. This is something I’ve been thinking about more and more, in part because I have a young child, but it feels like that is the sort of the moment where you’ve stopped learning in some fundamental way. You can still sort of incrementally learn.

But yeah, protecting that is something that’s, I think, really hard as you go through the world. I have to ask what your two contradictory superpowers are.

Joon Sung Park: There are a few different ways to phrase this. Um, but fundamentally, I am someone who is on day-to-day basis very concerned about many different things where we have to put every single thing in on the table to make sure that we succeed. But I’m also somebody, long term, who really do believe that the world is stacked for this team, that no matter what happens, we’ll actually succeed.

This particular trait I share very closely with one of my co-founders, uh, Lainie Yallen. Uh, Lainie is also somebody I observed. She is paranoid every day, and she’s always in the mindset of, we have to do every single thing possible today. Otherwise we’ll totally miss out on this opportunity, but have this very fundamental faith that no matter what happens, we will succeed.

I personally found this combination to be quite powerful, at least in the way that we were able to operate as a team and to the point of portrait artists painting their paintings. They sort of resemble them. I actually think team building is a lot like that too, where as a founder—myself, Lainie, Michael and Percy— we recruit people to a company and these people bring in their own unique talents that we do not have.

But at the same time, it is also us who are recruiting these people, who are finding these people to be compelling. In many ways, our belief as a founding team actually does get represented in the team in many ways. The team itself is also a self-portrait of who we are.

Joon Sung Park: So I do also think this is something that is broadly shared across the team.

Mario Gabriele: If you had unlimited resources and no operational constraints, what is the simulation you’d most like to run?

Joon Sung Park: I am deeply inspired by Thomas Schelling, the work and the career he led, and this was a scientist who had deep insight about the computation and the work of behavioral economics in particular, but also held deep interest in some of the largest societal problems that we face during those days. The simulation that we would be most interested in are also of that nature.

You look at our society today, what are the biggest societal problems that faces our community? It is climate change. It is the stability of our union. Can simulation create insights that would help us better navigate these really difficult, wicked problems? That really does inspire me and I ultimately want to believe that the final contribution that a company like Simile can make is one that is societal, that leads our community to be better, to be a more perfect union, than we are right now.

Mario Gabriele: If you could assign a book to everyone on Earth to read, what would you want to give to people? And if you want to throw a painting for, for everyone to look at, I would. I’d be very interested in that too. Okay.

Joon Sung Park: I think, um, what book ends up becoming meaningful to the individuals, I actually think is, you know, very personal. So, you know, I think everyone should find their own journey. The one that I actually had that had actually the most impact on me, actually, when I was younger, was The Catcher in the Rye by J. D. Salinger.

Without quite realizing, you know, it was very visceral representation of a young mind in the form of Holden Caulfield. And that always stuck with me. And I do think as a young person, I think I first read The Catcher in the Rye when I was, I want to say maybe 14, 15. I do think it actually had a fairly profound impact.

And I do believe it also had profound impact. You know, uh, to many people. Uh, so not necessarily recommending the book, but that’s the book that comes to my mind if I had to pick a title. There is a painting that I, um, that I have, uh, in my apartment, uh, a copy of it, because the real painting obviously is, you know, it’s, it’s, it’s very expensive and not available for sale is, of course, uh, is the triptych by Francis Bacon.

Uh, this is a triptych, but it’s three portraits that are painted side by side of Freud.

Uh, it’s one of the canonical pieces of Francis Bacon, and it’s very much in Francis Bacon style. He used to create these figure paintings, but he would distort the shape of the figures. He would smudge it. The eyes don’t quite align the right places. It’s, it’s very mysterious. But that actually was the painting that, you know, when I was an artist, I—of course, the style is—stylistically I was actually fairly far removed from Francis Bacon, but it was one of those pieces that I always admired. I’m like, uh, if I can paint something like this in the future, this would be an amazing contribution.

Mario Gabriele: Joon, this was so much fun. Thank you so much.

Joon Sung Park: Likewise. Thank you for having me.

For all past episodes and more, visit us at The Generalist Substack.

See you next time as we continue to explore the future.

news.article_content_zh:
“在[科幻小说中]描绘的任何真正先进的文明中，你确实看到了科学进步的两大支柱。一个是某种形式的通用人工智能，另一个是模拟。而我总是对模拟的想法更感兴趣。” – Joon Sung Park，Simile 联合创始人兼首席执行官

在我和朴俊成见面之前，他就模拟了对话。马里奥或像马里奥这样的人会问他什么问题？我觉得最值得深入研究的是什么？我不知道我对传真的坚持有多严格，尽管我希望如此。

琼在排练这些遭遇以及其他数千场遭遇方面具有优势。他是 Simile 的联合创始人兼首席执行官，Simile 是一家应用人工智能公司，致力于构建人类行为的基础模型。这涉及创建真人（如作家或播客）的数字双胞胎，并模拟他们对某些情况的反应。正如您可能想象的那样，这对许多公司来说是一个有吸引力的提议：例如，CVS Health 可以针对数千名模拟患者测试新的定价政策。银行可以在宣布费用调整之前模拟客户的反应。不过，Joon 的野心远远超出了这些案件，Simile 已筹集了超过 3 亿美元的资金来追求这些目标，最近的估值为 20 亿美元。

肖像画家总是画自己。我喜欢 Joon 的这句话，他本身就是一位有天赋的画家。当理解一件艺术作品时——无论何种媒介——我有时会忘记考虑它告诉我们关于作者而不是主题的信息。

“情感上的严谨。”我一直在听 Joon 的另一句话。他这样描述了为某人画一幅美丽的画所需要的强度。你需要建立这种深刻、严格的联系。我认为这是一个普遍的教训，在写作中尤其如此。

矛盾的超能力。另一个非常尖锐的启发式（你能看出我非常喜欢这次谈话吗？）。在招聘时，Joon 寻找的就是这样的人：具有两种很少同时具备的优势的人。例如，一位有着深厚的科学严肃性和非常顽皮的一面的同事。

向后工作。 Joon 的最终目标不是给 Simile 一个问题并让它做出预测。它是给出一个像气候变化这样的“邪恶”问题，并让它模拟大量可能的路径，以帮助我们找到最好的路径。

当一切都可以预测时谁会获胜？如果模拟像 Simile 所暗示的那样无处不在，那么公司如何相互竞争呢？ “战略”作为一门广泛的学科，是否已得到解决？ Joon 指出了关于边缘可能仍然存在的一些想法——即观点、专有数据和计算。当然，这只是一个思想实验。但这三者中的两家可能会为世界上资源最丰富的公司带来回报，但这远非理想。

当我问 Joon 他会给每个人分配哪本书时，他给大家起名叫《麦田里的守望者》，他第一次读这本书是在 14 或 15 岁左右。他小心翼翼地说，最重要的书都是非常个人化的，但霍尔顿·考尔菲尔德对年轻人内心的描绘却让他印象深刻。在我们谈话的早些时候，他还指出阿西莫夫的基础系列是《Simile》的核心灵感，特别是心理史学的想法：给模拟器一个理想的最终状态，并向后寻找那里的路径。

乔恩·罗森出版了一本新书《城堡》。我只读了几页，但考虑到我喜欢他所有其他奇异、随心所欲的调查，我怀疑我会非常喜欢它。

Grok Bot 在这一点上确实非常出色。我怀疑这种形式因素——由协调者监督的持久、主动、特定任务的机器人——将成为专业工作的默认形式。这是最接近拥有一群数字同事的事情。

Pharmaceutical leaders are skeptical of claims that AI could cure most diseases within a decade; the US FDA has yet to clear any AI-designed biotech drugs  —  No drug designed by artificial intelligence has won FDA clearance,

news.title: California accepts $1.42B in federal broadband funding, but challenges the Trump administration's demand that it stop enforcing state net neutrality rules (Jon Brodkin/Ars Technica)
news.title_en: California accepts $1.42B in federal broadband funding, but challenges the Trump administration's demand that it stop enforcing state net neutrality rules (Jon Brodkin/Ars Technica)
news.author: Ars Technica
news.article_content:
State tries to obtain broadband funds despite rejecting Trump admin condition.

California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration’s demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations.

California’s stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds.

The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction. California is slated to spend $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations, and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non-deployment projects.

State officials argue that California should be able to obtain the money and keep enforcing its laws because the Trump administration’s demand would violate the state’s constitutional rights. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) made its view clear in a carefully worded letter yesterday to Assistant Secretary of Commerce and NTIA Administrator Arielle Roth.

“The CPUC cannot be bound by any terms or conditions that are unconstitutional or not authorized by law and it expressly does not waive or concede any arguments or challenges concerning the legality, interpretation, or applicability of any term or condition,” CPUC President John Reynolds told Roth.

Reynolds’ letter also said the CPUC cannot prevent other California agencies from enforcing state laws, suggesting that the attorney general would maintain the right to punish misbehaving Internet providers.

Reynolds’ letter acknowledged that the NTIA may not agree with the CPUC’s stance and said the state thus will not distribute any funding to ISPs until after the state and federal agency sort out any differences. If the NTIA refuses to change its position, California could sue the Trump administration on the grounds that the condition is unconstitutional.

The NTIA does not appear likely to bend. “As noted in the Department’s response to CPUC, the terms and conditions of the award constitute the entire agreement between NTIA and CPUC. No part of the letter outlining CPUC’s concerns is incorporated into or made part of the award,” an NTIA spokesperson told Ars today.

Consumer advocacy group Public Knowledge supported CPUC’s position. The Trump administration’s demand to preempt state laws is “brazen and meritless,” the group said.

“This administration’s preposterous demand that industry be given a blanket waiver from affordability requirements, net neutrality and privacy protections, and any other commitments to connect and serve Americans has no basis in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), which established BEAD. And, as the commission points out, the NTIA has no authority to alter California state law or require California agencies to not enforce the law,” said Raza Panjwani, senior policy counsel at Public Knowledge.

The CPUC voted to ratify the funding plan in September. But Reynolds said in yesterday’s letter to the Trump administration that his agency’s acceptance of the funds is “based on the CPUC’s best understanding of the effect of Section 50” of the BEAD terms and conditions. Section 50 of the BEAD rules says each state:

shall commit that it will not enforce any law, regulation, order, contracting requirement, or other enforceable obligation that directly or indirectly regulates the rates, terms, and conditions of broadband Internet service… or imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules on broadband Internet service, against a Subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service within the State (i.e., both BEAD and non-BEAD locations), while that Subgrantee has any subgrant that is still within its period of performance, extended period of performance, or federal interest period.

The BEAD rules specify that a net neutrality rule is one prohibiting ISPs from “blocking content, throttling speeds, imposing data caps, or engaging in paid prioritization.” ISPs obtaining BEAD funding could be exempt from such laws for up to 14 years.

Reynolds’ letter said the NTIA-imposed condition is “vague and ambiguous as to its scope and its relationship to Section 47 U.S.C. § 1702(g)(2)(A)(i) of the BEAD statute,” the US law that created the BEAD program. He wrote:

The CPUC does not interpret Section 50 to require the CPUC to waive, release, or otherwise forfeit any rights, claims, arguments, or defenses concerning potential implications of Section 50 that may violate applicable laws. Further, the CPUC’s acceptance of funds under this award should not be understood as agreement either to refrain from compliance with mandatory legal duties or obligations, or to constrain other State of California entities in the exercise of their authorities to enforce state law, which is outside the scope of the CPUC’s authority. Moreover, California’s net neutrality law expressly provides that “any waiver of the provisions of this title is contrary to public policy and shall be unenforceable and void.” Likewise, many of the CPUC’s own programs that touch on broadband Internet access service are mandated by the California Public Utilities Code, and are neither discretionary nor waivable.

The NTIA today updated its BEAD progress dashboard to reflect that California has signed its final agreement with the federal agency. California was the last state or territory to turn in its final agreement.

“All 56 states and territories have signed and returned their award agreement, finalizing the process,” the NTIA’s updated dashboard page said.

California could face legal problems if and when it distributes the money, which is to be given to Internet service providers in exchange for deploying broadband in unserved and underserved areas. ISPs could insist that they don’t have to follow state law and sue California, or simply decide to violate consumer protection laws and defend against any lawsuits the state attorney general might file against them.

Reynolds apparently hopes to avoid that outcome by holding discussions with the NTIA to resolve any disagreement over the enforceability of California state law.

“To the extent that NTIA and the CPUC disagree about the CPUC’s obligations under Section 50 and other terms and conditions, the CPUC will execute any subgrant agreements if and when the CPUC and NTIA are able to resolve such disagreements and any other applicable conditions are met,” Reynolds wrote. “To that end, we will direct our staff to work diligently and cooperatively with NTIA staff to find such a solution.”

Whether California’s strategy works “depends on what happens next,” Stanford Law professor Barbara van Schewick, a longtime proponent of net neutrality and other telecom regulations, told Ars today.

“The letter doesn’t change the terms of California’s award: Condition 50 is still in it, and only a court or NTIA agreeing in writing can take it out,” she said. “The letter puts California’s position on the record before any contracts with providers are signed and preserves California’s legal arguments against Condition 50.”

Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office declined to comment when contacted by Ars today. A spokesperson for California Gov. Gavin Newsom said California is not giving up its right to enforce state laws against Internet providers.

“California is accepting federal broadband funding to bring high-speed Internet to hundreds of thousands of homes and businesses, many of them in rural and underserved communities,” a governor’s spokesperson said in a statement provided to Ars. “We’re ready to get these projects built with our local and federal partners. Connecting these communities is the goal, and so is protecting them. California’s laws, including our net neutrality protections, still stand.”

California’s net neutrality law prohibits ISPs from blocking or throttling lawful traffic and says ISPs may not require fees from websites or online services to deliver or prioritize their traffic to Internet users. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws, and California defeated ISPs that challenged the state law in court.

California also has a law that prohibits mobile providers from throttling first responders during emergencies. That law was passed in 2019, a year after Verizon throttled an “unlimited” data plan used by Santa Clara County firefighters during a wildfire. Local wildfire-preparedness groups warned that the BEAD condition could prevent California from enforcing the throttling law and requirements for battery backups on cell towers.

According to van Schewick, “California has strong arguments that Condition 50 is illegal. Congress designed BEAD to get broadband built while making sure the providers who take the money follow the law: the statute directs states to ensure funded providers can carry out their work ‘in compliance with all applicable Federal, State, and local laws.’”

But van Schewick said the letter is just an initial step. “The real test comes the first time a BEAD provider blocks a competitor’s app, throttles firefighters, or walks away from a price commitment,” she said. “If the state enforces its laws when that happens, the letter will have protected Californians. If the state looks the other way, Condition 50 will have worked exactly as the providers intended, without a single court ever ruling on it.”
news.original_content:
State tries to obtain broadband funds despite rejecting Trump admin condition.

California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration’s demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations.

California’s stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds.

The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction. California is slated to spend $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations, and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non-deployment projects.

State officials argue that California should be able to obtain the money and keep enforcing its laws because the Trump administration’s demand would violate the state’s constitutional rights. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) made its view clear in a carefully worded letter yesterday to Assistant Secretary of Commerce and NTIA Administrator Arielle Roth.

“The CPUC cannot be bound by any terms or conditions that are unconstitutional or not authorized by law and it expressly does not waive or concede any arguments or challenges concerning the legality, interpretation, or applicability of any term or condition,” CPUC President John Reynolds told Roth.

Reynolds’ letter also said the CPUC cannot prevent other California agencies from enforcing state laws, suggesting that the attorney general would maintain the right to punish misbehaving Internet providers.

Reynolds’ letter acknowledged that the NTIA may not agree with the CPUC’s stance and said the state thus will not distribute any funding to ISPs until after the state and federal agency sort out any differences. If the NTIA refuses to change its position, California could sue the Trump administration on the grounds that the condition is unconstitutional.

The NTIA does not appear likely to bend. “As noted in the Department’s response to CPUC, the terms and conditions of the award constitute the entire agreement between NTIA and CPUC. No part of the letter outlining CPUC’s concerns is incorporated into or made part of the award,” an NTIA spokesperson told Ars today.

Consumer advocacy group Public Knowledge supported CPUC’s position. The Trump administration’s demand to preempt state laws is “brazen and meritless,” the group said.

“This administration’s preposterous demand that industry be given a blanket waiver from affordability requirements, net neutrality and privacy protections, and any other commitments to connect and serve Americans has no basis in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), which established BEAD. And, as the commission points out, the NTIA has no authority to alter California state law or require California agencies to not enforce the law,” said Raza Panjwani, senior policy counsel at Public Knowledge.

The CPUC voted to ratify the funding plan in September. But Reynolds said in yesterday’s letter to the Trump administration that his agency’s acceptance of the funds is “based on the CPUC’s best understanding of the effect of Section 50” of the BEAD terms and conditions. Section 50 of the BEAD rules says each state:

shall commit that it will not enforce any law, regulation, order, contracting requirement, or other enforceable obligation that directly or indirectly regulates the rates, terms, and conditions of broadband Internet service… or imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules on broadband Internet service, against a Subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service within the State (i.e., both BEAD and non-BEAD locations), while that Subgrantee has any subgrant that is still within its period of performance, extended period of performance, or federal interest period.

The BEAD rules specify that a net neutrality rule is one prohibiting ISPs from “blocking content, throttling speeds, imposing data caps, or engaging in paid prioritization.” ISPs obtaining BEAD funding could be exempt from such laws for up to 14 years.

Reynolds’ letter said the NTIA-imposed condition is “vague and ambiguous as to its scope and its relationship to Section 47 U.S.C. § 1702(g)(2)(A)(i) of the BEAD statute,” the US law that created the BEAD program. He wrote:

The CPUC does not interpret Section 50 to require the CPUC to waive, release, or otherwise forfeit any rights, claims, arguments, or defenses concerning potential implications of Section 50 that may violate applicable laws. Further, the CPUC’s acceptance of funds under this award should not be understood as agreement either to refrain from compliance with mandatory legal duties or obligations, or to constrain other State of California entities in the exercise of their authorities to enforce state law, which is outside the scope of the CPUC’s authority. Moreover, California’s net neutrality law expressly provides that “any waiver of the provisions of this title is contrary to public policy and shall be unenforceable and void.” Likewise, many of the CPUC’s own programs that touch on broadband Internet access service are mandated by the California Public Utilities Code, and are neither discretionary nor waivable.

The NTIA today updated its BEAD progress dashboard to reflect that California has signed its final agreement with the federal agency. California was the last state or territory to turn in its final agreement.

“All 56 states and territories have signed and returned their award agreement, finalizing the process,” the NTIA’s updated dashboard page said.

California could face legal problems if and when it distributes the money, which is to be given to Internet service providers in exchange for deploying broadband in unserved and underserved areas. ISPs could insist that they don’t have to follow state law and sue California, or simply decide to violate consumer protection laws and defend against any lawsuits the state attorney general might file against them.

Reynolds apparently hopes to avoid that outcome by holding discussions with the NTIA to resolve any disagreement over the enforceability of California state law.

“To the extent that NTIA and the CPUC disagree about the CPUC’s obligations under Section 50 and other terms and conditions, the CPUC will execute any subgrant agreements if and when the CPUC and NTIA are able to resolve such disagreements and any other applicable conditions are met,” Reynolds wrote. “To that end, we will direct our staff to work diligently and cooperatively with NTIA staff to find such a solution.”

Whether California’s strategy works “depends on what happens next,” Stanford Law professor Barbara van Schewick, a longtime proponent of net neutrality and other telecom regulations, told Ars today.

“The letter doesn’t change the terms of California’s award: Condition 50 is still in it, and only a court or NTIA agreeing in writing can take it out,” she said. “The letter puts California’s position on the record before any contracts with providers are signed and preserves California’s legal arguments against Condition 50.”

Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office declined to comment when contacted by Ars today. A spokesperson for California Gov. Gavin Newsom said California is not giving up its right to enforce state laws against Internet providers.

“California is accepting federal broadband funding to bring high-speed Internet to hundreds of thousands of homes and businesses, many of them in rural and underserved communities,” a governor’s spokesperson said in a statement provided to Ars. “We’re ready to get these projects built with our local and federal partners. Connecting these communities is the goal, and so is protecting them. California’s laws, including our net neutrality protections, still stand.”

California’s net neutrality law prohibits ISPs from blocking or throttling lawful traffic and says ISPs may not require fees from websites or online services to deliver or prioritize their traffic to Internet users. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws, and California defeated ISPs that challenged the state law in court.

California also has a law that prohibits mobile providers from throttling first responders during emergencies. That law was passed in 2019, a year after Verizon throttled an “unlimited” data plan used by Santa Clara County firefighters during a wildfire. Local wildfire-preparedness groups warned that the BEAD condition could prevent California from enforcing the throttling law and requirements for battery backups on cell towers.

According to van Schewick, “California has strong arguments that Condition 50 is illegal. Congress designed BEAD to get broadband built while making sure the providers who take the money follow the law: the statute directs states to ensure funded providers can carry out their work ‘in compliance with all applicable Federal, State, and local laws.’”

But van Schewick said the letter is just an initial step. “The real test comes the first time a BEAD provider blocks a competitor’s app, throttles firefighters, or walks away from a price commitment,” she said. “If the state enforces its laws when that happens, the letter will have protected Californians. If the state looks the other way, Condition 50 will have worked exactly as the providers intended, without a single court ever ruling on it.”

news.article_content_zh:
尽管拒绝特朗普的行政条件，该州仍试图获得宽带资金。

加州正在接受特朗普政府提供的 14.2 亿美元宽带拨款资金，但该州没有接受特朗普政府要求其停止执行网络中立法和其他电信法规的要求。

加州反对特朗普政府的立场可能会导致涉及州、联邦政府和寻求政府资金的互联网提供商的多起法律诉讼。尽管加州告诉联邦政府它将接受这笔钱，但它保留质疑美国施加的条件的权利。该州可能会推迟或取消分配宽带拨款的计划，具体取决于进程的进展情况。

美国国家电信和信息管理局 (NTIA) 去年决定，各州必须同意不对从 420 亿美元宽带公平、接入和部署 (BEAD) 计划中获得资金的 ISP 实施任何费率监管或网络中立规则。尽管存在这一限制，加州仍必须决定是否接受其在该基金中的份额。加州计划斥资 14.2 亿美元在 270,571 个地点部署宽带，最终可能从 BEAD 获得高达 18.6 亿美元的部署和非部署项目。

州官员认为，加州应该能够获得这笔资金并继续执行其法律，因为特朗普政府的要求将侵犯该州的宪法权利。加州公用事业委员会 (CPUC) 昨天在致助理商务部长兼 NTIA 局长 Arielle Roth 的一封措辞谨慎的信中明确表达了自己的观点。

“CPUC 不受任何违宪或未经法律授权的条款或条件的约束，并且明确不会放弃或承认任何有关任何条款或条件的合法性、解释或适用性的争论或质疑，”CPUC 主席约翰·雷诺兹 (John Reynolds) 告诉罗斯。

雷诺兹的信中还表示，CPUC 无法阻止加州其他机构执行州法律，这表明总检察长将保留惩罚行为不当的互联网提供商的权利。

雷诺兹在信中承认 NTIA 可能不同意 CPUC 的立场，并表示在州和联邦机构解决任何分歧之前，州不会向 ISP 分配任何资金。如果 NTIA 拒绝改变立场，加州可能会以该条件违宪为由起诉特朗普政府。

NTIA 似乎不太可能弯曲。 NTIA 发言人今天告诉 Ars：“正如该部门对 CPUC 的回应中所指出的，该裁决的条款和条件构成了 NTIA 与 CPUC 之间的完整协议。信中概述 CPUC 担忧的任何部分均未纳入该裁决或成为该裁决的一部分。”

消费者权益倡导组织 Public Knowledge 支持 CPUC 的立场。该组织表示，特朗普政府要求优先于各州法律的要求是“厚颜无耻且毫无根据的”。

Public Knowledge 高级政策顾问 Raza Panjwani 表示：“本届政府荒谬地要求行业全面豁免承受能力要求、网络中立性和隐私保护以及任何其他连接和服务美国人的承诺，这在建立 BEAD 的基础设施投资和就业法案 (IIJA) 中没有任何依据。而且，正如委员会指出的那样，NTIA 无权改变加州法律或要求加州机构不执行法律。”

CPUC 于 9 月投票批准了该资助计划。但雷诺兹在昨天给特朗普政府的信中表示，他的机构接受这笔资金是“基于 CPUC 对 BEAD 条款和条件第 50 条影响的最佳理解”。 BEAD 规则第 50 条规定，每个州：

应承诺，当子受让人拥有仍处于其履行期限、延长期限内的任何分赠款时，不会对子受让人或其在州内提供服务的任何地方（即 BEAD 和非 BEAD 地点）的附属机构执行任何直接或间接规范宽带互联网服务的费率、条款和条件的法律、法规、命令、合同要求或其他可执行义务……或对宽带互联网服务强加网络中立规则、开放接入或其他公用事业风格的规则。绩效或联邦利息期。

BEAD 规则规定，网络中立性规则是禁止 ISP“阻止内容、限制速度、施加数据上限或参与付费优先级”的规则。获得 BEAD 资助的 ISP 可以在长达 14 年的时间内免受此类法律的约束。

【起因与机理】为了既能拿到联邦基建资金解决偏远地区网络覆盖，又不想丢掉州政府对互联网服务商的监管主权

news.title: Following backlash against its education updates, Google says schools can choose to enable Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually (Isabel O'Brien/CNBC)
news.title_en: Following backlash against its education updates, Google says schools can choose to enable Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually (Isabel O'Brien/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
Google is playing defense on Tuesday after a political backlash to its new policy surrounding use of artificial intelligence in schools.

In a blog post titled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Google said it's bringing AI into its Classroom offering with a product called Guided Learning. The New York Times published a story saying that the company will turn off search for schools that reject AI entirely.

Following the Times' story, prominent left-leaning politicians, including Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced their outrage on social media.

"Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," Mamdani wrote on X. Sanders wrote that "Google is threatening schools," referring to the policy as "extortion."

Google responded later in the day. In a post on X, the company said its new policy was meant to give schools more choice over how students interact with AI. Google said its Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and search are turned off by default, and that "schools are in control," with the ability to turn them as they see fit.

"We are also updating Search for schools to make it better for learning," Google wrote. "Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don't get quick answers to schoolwork."

The company's post didn't explicitly respond to the claim that access to search requires use of AI. However, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated."

A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to the X post when asked for comment.

Google's broader practices have come under fire in recent years, with the company losing antitrust cases over its search and advertising businesses. Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan aggressively pursued Google and other tech giants, including Meta and Amazon.

Khan said in a post on X on Tuesday that Google's new AI for learning policy highlights "the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service."

It's the latest controversy related to the impact of technology on children and the role leading internet companies are playing in delivering information.

In August, Meta reached a landmark $16.7 billion settlement in its child safety trial after a number of state attorneys general accused the company of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps like Facebook and Instagram.

The same month, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens after state attorneys general launched an investigation into the company's safety practices, with Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican, filing a lawsuit in June.

The nonprofit Common Sense Media recently gave Google's AI overviews an "unacceptable risk" rating. Last month, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo., launched an inquiry over Google's push of AI into classrooms.

Google introduced AI overviews as a search function in May 2024.

— CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report.

WATCH: Meta settled its child safety lawsuit. Now comes the hard part.

news.title_zh: 谷歌面对教育界反弹修改AI入校策略
news.summary_zh: 因强制AI入校遭政客指控垄断与威胁，谷歌紧急改口允许学校独立开关各项AI功能

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌在因强制AI入校政策遭遇参议员伯尼·桑德斯等政客指责其涉嫌垄断与“勒索”后，于官方博客及社交媒体迅速做出防御性调整。谷歌明确宣布，旗下的Gemini聊天机器人、Gemini Notebook以及搜索服务在学校默认处于关闭状态，各学校可根据自身需求自由选择单独开启某项功能。此举起因于此前媒体披露其对拒绝AI的学校采取关闭搜索等强硬限制，引发了巨大的政治反弹与舆论压力。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Google faced intense backlash from politicians over its AI-in-schools policy, prompting the company to clarify that schools can now enable Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually by default. The controversy arose after reports suggested Google would restrict search for schools rejecting AI entirely, leading accusations of monopolistic coercion.

elements_en.what: Google backpedaled after coercion accusations, stating schools can independently toggle Gemini, Notebook, or Search

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 大厂本来想借着“关掉全家桶”强行帮祖国的花朵提前适应AI内卷，结果刚一动手就被政客们当成了靶子。眼看勒索大棒还没挥出去就砸了自己脚，公关部只能连夜把开关拆下来塞回学校手里。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Google tried to force-feed AI to the next generation by locking the classroom door, only to get smacked down by politicians screaming monopoly. Facing instant PR shrapnel, they quickly handed the remote control back to the schools before the anti-trust pitchforks came out.

news.article_content_zh:
谷歌周二在学校使用人工智能的新政策遭到政治强烈反对后，采取了防御措施。

谷歌在一篇题为“为学习设计负责任的人工智能”的博客文章中表示，它将通过一款名为“引导学习”的产品将人工智能引入其课堂产品。 《纽约时报》发表报道称，该公司将停止搜索完全拒绝人工智能的学校。

在《泰晤士报》报道后，包括佛蒙特州参议员伯尼·桑德斯和纽约市长佐兰·马姆达尼在内的著名左倾政客在社交媒体上表达了他们的愤怒。

Mamdani 在 X 上写道：“谷歌正试图利用其垄断力量迫使人工智能进入我们的公立学校。”桑德斯写道，“谷歌正在威胁学校”，并将该政策称为“勒索”。

谷歌当天晚些时候做出了回应。该公司在 X 上的一篇帖子中表示，其新政策旨在让学校在学生与人工智能互动的方式上有更多选择。谷歌表示，其 Gemini 聊天机器人、Gemini Notebook 和搜索默认情况下处于关闭状态，并且“学校处于控制之中”，可以根据需要关闭它们。

谷歌写道：“我们还在更新学校搜索，以使其更好地学习。” “具体来说，人工智能模式和人工智能概述将通过问题提供逐步指导学习，这样学生就不会快速获得作业的答案。”

该公司的帖子没有明确回应访问搜索需要使用人工智能的说法。然而，谷歌教育副总裁克里斯·菲利普斯(Chris Phillips)告诉《泰晤士报》，“搜索和人工智能是深度融合的。”

当被要求置评时，谷歌发言人向 CNBC 推荐了 X 帖子。

近年来，谷歌更广泛的做法受到了批评，该公司在搜索和广告业务方面输掉了反垄断诉讼。前联邦贸易委员会主席莉娜·汗 (Lina Khan) 积极追捧谷歌和其他科技巨头，包括 Meta 和亚马逊。

Khan 周二在 X 上发帖称，谷歌新的人工智能学习政策凸显了“允许不受监管的垄断者控制基本服务的危险”。

这是有关技术对儿童的影响以及领先的互联网公司在传递信息方面所扮演的角色的最新争议。

8 月，Meta 在儿童安全审判中达成了具有里程碑意义的 167 亿美元和解协议，此前一些州总检察长指控该公司歪曲了 Facebook 和 Instagram 等应用程序对儿童心理健康造成的伤害程度。

同月，在各州总检察长对该公司的安全实践发起调查后，OpenAI 推出了针对青少年的 ChatGPT，佛罗里达州总检察长、共和党人 James Uthmeier 于 6 月提起诉讼。

非营利组织 Common Sense Media 最近给予谷歌的人工智能概述“不可接受的风险”评级。上个月，康涅狄格州民主党参议员理查德·布卢门撒尔 (Richard Blumenthal) 和密苏里州共和党参议员乔什·霍利 (Josh Hawley) 对谷歌将人工智能推入课堂的行为发起了调查。

celebrity.title_en:
The AI layoff gamble is backfiring.

Companies that rushed to replace workers with AI are now cleaning up the mess, per The Guardian.

Meta scaled back plans to cut staff and use more AI agents after employees spent growing time cleaning up the agents’ technical and security errors. It’s now rehiring managers.
Microsoft and McKinsey are limiting employee AI use as costs pile up.
Walmart workers say AI scheduling and task tools set impossible standards and generate false alerts.

The payoff isn’t showing up: 90% of executives say AI hasn’t yet boosted productivity at their companies, per an Atlanta Fed working paper.

Yet more than 112,000 US job cuts this year have cited AI, per Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

celebrity.title_en:
ANTHROPIC IS NOW IN DAMAGE CONTROL 🚨

Less than a week after the “no game recreations” rule showed up in Claude Code, Anthropic quietly rewrote it. Same server flag, “tengu_heron_brook”.

Two things got added:
• “or with similar mechanics”: copying a game’s gameplay is now explicitly allowed
• “(its name, characters, art, music, levels or look)”: now spells out what actually counts as a “recreation”

They also added a second flag, “original_games_guidance”, and Claude Code 2.1.317 now has the new wording built straight into the app.

Still no setting to turn it off.

celebrity.title:
Publicly funded science should work more like open source software.

Today a result is a PDF. The data often isn't share
celebrity.title_en:
Publicly funded science should work more like open source software.

Today a result is a PDF. The data often isn't shared, the code isn't public, and few studies ever get replicated.

Imagine every experiment as a repo. Data, code, and protocol, all versioned. Anyone could fork it, rerun it, and send a fix. Funders could reward replications as much as new papers.

AI makes this urgent. Agents are now making more discoveries than ever. The bottleneck becomes replication/validation. Then commercialization, which still requires moving atoms in the real world and meetings with regulators.
celebrity.title_zh:
公共资助的科学应该更像开源软件。

今天的结果是 PDF。数据通常不共享，代码不公开，而且很少有研究能够被复制。

将每个实验想象成一个存储库。数据、代码和协议，全部版本化。任何人都可以分叉它、重新运行它并发送修复程序。资助者可以像奖励新论

celebrity.content_snippet:
Publicly funded science should work more like open source software.

Today a result is a PDF. The data often isn't shared, the code isn't public, and few studies ever get replicated.

Imagine every experiment as a repo. Data, code, and protocol, all versioned. Anyone could fork it, rerun it, and send a fix. Funders could reward replications as much as new papers.

AI makes this urgent. Agents are now making more discoveries than ever. The bottleneck becomes replication/validation. Then commercialization, which still requires moving atoms in the real world and meetings with regulators.

celebrity.title_en:
Several comments:
1. image/video SSL methods differ by whether they use reconstruction or not. Joint embedding architectures Amy or may not have a predictor (JEA vs JEPA). They also differ by their anti-collapse method and data corruption/augmentation methods.
2. DINO *is* a kind of JEPA (technically a JEA). The difference with other JEPA models is the anti-collapse criterion (based on contrative clustering+ stopgradient/EMA), and the data augmentation scheme (image transformations, which is task specific),
3. V-JEPA 2.1, like DINO, is from Meta-FAIR (corporate lab), involved significant engineering teams, large/proprietary datasets, considerable computing resources, lots of fine-tuning, and number-pushing on many benchmarks.
4. Many JEPA papers are applications and/or fine-tuned versions of DINO, V-JEPA or I-JEPA.
5. LeJEPA, LeWM, and most other papers with "JEPA" in the title are *research* papers focused on the methodology, often done by students in academic labs, involving no engineering support, very little computing resources, and small/public training sets. They are generally tested on toy problems, simulated environments, or small/public benchmarks.
6. You simply cannot compare 5 with 2/3/4. 5 gives you ideas and new methods, not models. 2/3 give you well-engineered models, with lots of empirically validated tricks. Only rarely will 2/3 give you a new, well-principled method with room to spare. 5 give you empirical results on new applications.
7. What is published in 5 are methods that will eventually become like 2 and 3, whenever someone with resources picks it up and scales it.

DO NOT CONFUSE UPSTREAM FOUNDATIONAL RESEARCH ON METHODS AND DOWNSTREAM SCALING -> ENGINEERING -> NUMBER PUSHING -> MODELS -> PRODUCTS.
The former makes the rest possible, but it takes time.

2. DINO *是*一种 JEPA（技术上是 JEA）。与其他JEPA模型的区别在于抗崩溃准则（基于对比聚类+ stopgradient / EMA），以及数据增强方案（图像变换，这是特定于任务的），
3. V-JEPA 2.1 与 DINO 一样，来自 Meta-FAIR（企业实验室），涉及重要的工程团队、大型/专有数据集、大量计算资源、大量微调以及许多基准上的数字推送。
4. 许多 JEPA 论文是 DINO、V-JEPA 或 I-JEPA 的应用程序和/或微调版本。
5. LeJEPA、LeWM 和大多数其他标题中带有“JEPA”的论文都是专注于方法论的“研究”论文，通常由学生在学术实验室中完成，不涉及工程支持、很少的计算资源和小型/公共训练集。它们通常在玩具问题、模拟环境或小型/公共基准测试上进行测试。
6. 你根本无法将 5 与 2/3/4 进行比较。 5 给你的是想法和新方法，而不是模型。 2/3 为您提供精心设计的模型，其中包含许多经过经验验证的技巧。只有极少数情况下，2/3 的人才会为您提供一种新的、原则性良好且有余地的方法。 5 为您提供新应用的实证结果。
7. 5 中发布的方法最终将变得像 2 和 3 一样，只要有资源的人拿起它并扩展它。

不要混淆上游方法的基础研究和下游扩展 -> 工程 -> 数字推送 -> 模型 -> 产品。
前者使其余的成为可能，但这需要时间。

Working on Claude Code, he says
celebrity.title_en:
Anthropic engineer Addy Osmani warns that AI could make us stop thinking for ourselves.

Working on Claude Code, he says AI agents now handle so much of his work that he rarely needs to use critical thinking.

He identifies three stages: “cognitive offloading” (delegating tasks), “deferral” (accepting AI answers) and “cognitive surrender” (trusting AI completely).

“Skills that you stop exercising are going to go away, and probably faster than you might guess.”

他在 Claude Code 工作时表示，人工智能代理现在处理了他的大部分工作，他很少需要使用批判性思维。

他确定了三个阶段：“认知卸载”

Anthropic engineer Addy Osmani warns that AI could make us stop thinking for ourselves.

Example for the intellectually challenged. 

We have 5 polling units in your street. All 5 polling units vote for say NDC and votes are 500 votes from those polling units, right?

Time to collate and they bring out results for 9 polling units with their pumped results.

celebrity.title_en:
SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government. 

And I need to be close to the factories, so that I can walk the floor in person. That’s why the first major SpaceX factory was in LA and first major Tesla factory was in SF Bay Area.

As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas.
celebrity.title_zh:
SpaceX 和特斯拉在德克萨斯州蓬勃发展，因为我们并没有一直在一个压迫性和榨取性的州政府下运营。

而且我需要靠近工厂，这样我才能亲自到工厂走一走。这就是为什么 SpaceX 的第一家大型工厂位于洛杉矶，特斯拉的第一家大型工厂位于旧金山

celebrity.content_snippet:

celebrity.title_en:
Claude Code can design furniture part by part and then give you a bill of materials to order each part and put it together yourself 

And way cheaper than big interior brands sell you their furniture

Furnishing my house I discovered how absolutely insane prices are for the most basic cheap materials put together with a fancy brand tied to it

One shop had a sofa for $30,000 😂

I think with Opus 5.5 and other models easily operating 3d programs like Blender and FreeCAD (both free) it makes more sense to cut out the middle man and go straight to suppliers and design and build your own furniture

Which in a way makes customers more powerful (they can get exactly what they want and usually for cheaper without the markup)

Anyway @theannalux designed this table from scratch, she's not a furniture designer, not a coder, she just had an idea of a style and worked with Claude Code in the terminal (far superior to the app I will keep saying this)

If you design your own furniture and buy the raw materials directly, you can save 85% compared to premium brands like Poliform

That means the $30,000 sofa becomes $4,500! And the $8,000 dinner table becomes just $1,200!

You can see where the idea comes from that AI will make everything 5x to 20x cheaper, and it's already starting!

What happens when
celebrity.title_en:
The Agent Economy Needs Real Usage

There is an important question behind every AI-agent ecosystem :

What happens when people actually start using the agent's ?

For @meetmotes, this question connects directly to its planned protocol economics

Motes proposes a 1% service fee on defined eligible agent activity

The idea is to create a relationship between agent usage and protocol revenue, with the planned revenue supporting protocol operations and $MOTES buy-backs

I find this model interesting because it places actual activity at the centre of the ecosystem

The NFT establishes the agent identity.
The smart account provides the asset infrastructure

The agent performs authorised actions within owner-defined limits

Eligible activity can contribute to the protocol economy

It's a clear ownership-to-usage-to-revenue narrative

Of course, the final fee rules and revenue allocation will determine how the model works in practice

For an agent economy to be sustainable, useful activity needs a well-defined economic foundation

One NFT, One Agent, A protocol economy built around real agent activity
