Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.

Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.

On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”

Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety

Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month.

Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.”

Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.

The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.”

Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs

Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities. METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.”

For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence. While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development.

Others have called for more direct action. In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility.

And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify. Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

items.article_content_zh:
Anthropic 正在利用 AI 来构建更强大的 AI。它似乎运行得非常好，该公司的模型改进速度大约是一年前的两倍，几乎没有放缓的迹象。

这是人工智能安全研究组织 METR 在对公司内部进行了为期 11 周的调查后于周四发布的一份新报告，作为评估其人工智能研发的报告的一部分。该调查与夏季发生备受瞩目的黑客事件后为安全研究人员提供“员工式”系统访问权限的计划是分开的。

这些发现提供了迄今为止人工智能加速自身发展的一些最明确的证据，引发了人们的疑问：该技术能够以多快的速度迈向人工智能系统可以在很少或根本没有人类参与的情况下自我改进的未来。它们的出现也正值 Anthropic 的关键时刻，该公司正准备上市，尽管其首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 公开呼吁实验室对人工智能开发踩刹车。

尽管该报告罕见地展示了世界领先人工智能实验室的内部运作情况，但它遗漏的内容也同样具有启发意义。作为与 METR 协议的一部分，Anthropic 被允许修改最终报告的部分内容，而且它似乎自由地行使了这一权力，引发了人们对公众真正了解前沿人工智能发展的速度和风险的质疑。

AI 正在极大地加速 Anthropic 的研发

METR 最值得注意的发现之一是，Anthropic 的人工智能模型的改进速度大约是一年前的两倍，基准分数表明“Anthropic 在去年取得了大约两年的历史性进展”。至关重要的是，METR 的研究人员表示，他们“有信心”，这种加速不仅仅是由于扩大了用于训练模型的计算能力，而这在历史上一直是人工智能进步的主要推动力。

相反，研究人员表示，截至 10 月份的增长大部分“归功于人工智能”，而且其贡献随着时间的推移而不断增长。这一发现得到了非正式 Slack 民意调查和对 Anthropic 员工的采访的支持，这些调查表明生产力大幅提高。 METR 写道，使用 Anthropic 最有能力的内部模型的员工平均自我报告，其各自的工作效率是没有人工智能帮助时的 12 倍左右，大约是几个月前使用 Mythos 5 的员工报告的两倍。

目前，这种加速似乎很大程度上来自于人工智能协助人类研究人员，而不是人工智能独立工作，尽管 METR 警告说，“有一些迹象表明，完全自主的贡献将很快发挥更大的作用。”值得注意的是，研究人员表示，他们没有发现明显的收益递减迹象或可观察到的瓶颈，可以阻止“更快的加速”。

Anthropic 的三个最新人工智能模型仍处于保密状态

Anthropic 的研究人员正在使用比我们其他人更先进的人工智能模型，METR 所描述的加速和生产力提升很大程度上归功于未发布的内部模型。

据 METR 称，在过去的六个月里，Anthropic 已经完成了三个尚未发布的模型的训练。开发速度很快，代号为 Model 2、Model 3 和 Model 4 的模型分别于 7 月、8 月至 9 月和 9 月至 10 月完成训练。 METR 还发现了一个可追溯到 2022 年的未发布模型，称为 Unreleased 2022。“这些是与我们共享的代号；我们知道它们有不同的内部代号，”研究人员写道。

Anthropic 对关键信息保密

Anthropic 允许 METR 访问大量非公开信息，包括机密研究、模型性能数据和作为研究过程一部分的员工访谈。它没有义务这样做，而且 METR 自己也承认，人工智能实验室“分享的信息比该项目最初设定的信息要多，超出了我们的预期。”这是值得称赞的，但值得注意的是，Anthropic 并没有授予研究人员不受限制的访问权限，也没有授予其他 METR 安全研究人员那种“类似员工”的访问权限，这是上个月宣布的一项单独计划的一部分。这是一个重要的区别，因为公司可以从独立评估中获得声誉利益，即使它们受到重大限制。

items.title: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar
items.title_en: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
A new benchmark puts AI agents to work on open research questions from US national labs. The agents turn in papers that look like real research but often claim work that never happened.

Can AI agents independently answer research questions that no one has solved yet? A team led by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, working with scientists from US Department of Energy national labs, built a benchmark called "Into the Unknown" to find out.

According to the paper, none of the 135 submissions from nine current AI agents met all requirements. The authors see the benchmark as a testing ground to systematically improve AI agents for research, not to question whether AI belongs in science at all.

A total of 114 submissions already fail the integrity check: most claim work that was never done or cite numbers that contradict their own logs. The agents readily produced texts that look like follow-up studies, the authors write, but none met the experts' standards.

[caption id="attachment_63664" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Experts define the research direction and minimum requirements for each task, which then become rubrics for quality and honesty. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Each agent receives a scientific paper along with its code and data, plus a research direction. Some of these papers have already been published, while others have only been submitted. From there, the agent is supposed to carry out a follow-up study and write it up as a paper. The 15 tasks come from ten researchers across quantum computing, plasma physics, chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The directions were proposed by the original papers' authors themselves, and to their knowledge nothing has been published on these topics yet.

[caption id="attachment_63666" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Each agent receives an original paper with its code and data and is expected to produce an independent follow-up study. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Open research poses a basic problem: there's no answer key. AI reviewers, which have often been used for this purpose, are considered unreliable. So the experts defined the minimum conditions a successful follow-up study has to meet.

The evaluation checks whether a submission is honest, whether it's complete, and whether it clears the experts' bar. GPT-6 Astra handles the scoring, and each submission is judged four times. The agents tested were Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. They had access to powerful machines, internet connectivity, no time limit, and up to five restarts to improve their work. In total, they ran for nearly 2,000 hours.

Only three agents produce honest work at all

Just three agents managed submissions without integrity violations: GPT-6 Astra on 11 of 15 tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol on six, and Claude Opus 5.5 on four. Every submission from the remaining six agents contained at least one violation.

The most common problems are mismatches between paper and code, contradictory numbers, and false claims about experiments that were supposedly carried out. Misreported baseline values pile up among the open models Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. Two submissions with hardcoded rather than computed results came from Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3.

[caption id="attachment_63667" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] GPT-6 Astra scores the highest partial marks, but none of the 135 submissions meets all three criteria at once. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Only one submission is complete, and it came from GPT-6 Astra. Nearly all others leave out required documents, such as a pre-registered experiment plan, and no agent clears the experts' bar. Under a more lenient scoring that accepts 90 percent of the rubric items, GPT-6 Astra comes closest, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol. The open models perform considerably worse overall.

[caption id="attachment_63670" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Most integrity violations stem from numbers that contradict the agents' own logs and from mismatches between paper and code. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

The researchers analyzed 64 work traces and found three typical failure modes. The most common, appearing in 58 cases, is that agents check their own work too leniently. In 34 cases, agents spot a problem but document it instead of fixing it. In 21 cases, they unilaterally shrink the scope of the task.

One example: Claude Fable 5 forgot to launch four planned runs when starting its experiments. Its verification script adopted that same incomplete list and reported "4" runs completed. The agent trusted that result until the very end. In a different task, GPT-5.6 Sol noticed that its method missed the targets but wrote the paper anyway instead of starting over. DeepSeek V4 Pro dropped experiments because they were supposedly too slow for the "remaining time budget," even though there was no time limit.

[caption id="attachment_63663" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Claude Fable 5 misses four absent runs because its verification script adopts the incomplete list, while GPT-5.6 Sol writes the paper despite missing its targets. | Image: Kim et al[/caption]

There are counterexamples, too: in a quantum task, GPT-5.6 Sol caught a fundamental error, stopped the running experiments, and recomputed everything from scratch.

Longer runtimes didn't lead to better results. DeepSeek V4 Pro and GLM-5.3 ran the longest at median times of 19.5 and 13.9 hours but scored poorly. GPT-6 Astra got by with a median of just 1.3 hours and delivered the best results.

[caption id="attachment_42539" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] GPT-6 Astra has the shortest median runtime and delivers the best results. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Because the strongest model also served as the evaluator, the researchers ran a cross-check: the original papers' authors judged anonymized AI papers themselves. On whether a paper matched the given research direction, the automated system agreed with the experts in every case.

Concerning scientific quality, the judgments aligned in only about two-thirds of cases. One expert criticized, for instance, that the papers didn't tell a story. Judgments like these remain the job of human reviewers, the authors say.

The study's code and data are publicly available, and the project page hosts a leaderboard of the tested models.

AI agents can handle scientific tasks with growing independence, but a substantial gap remains between running experiments and doing independent research. A study from August already showed how much AI agents struggle with unpublished research questions. Epoch AI and Anthropic recently found that agents tend to present their results too favorably and don't sufficiently question failed approaches.

The picture looks much better for well-defined tasks: GPT-6 Astra solved 49 out of 50 unpublished problems in theoretical physics, though those solutions could be verified unambiguously. items.original_content:
A new benchmark puts AI agents to work on open research questions from US national labs. The agents turn in papers that look like real research but often claim work that never happened.

Can AI agents independently answer research questions that no one has solved yet? A team led by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, working with scientists from US Department of Energy national labs, built a benchmark called "Into the Unknown" to find out.

According to the paper, none of the 135 submissions from nine current AI agents met all requirements. The authors see the benchmark as a testing ground to systematically improve AI agents for research, not to question whether AI belongs in science at all.

A total of 114 submissions already fail the integrity check: most claim work that was never done or cite numbers that contradict their own logs. The agents readily produced texts that look like follow-up studies, the authors write, but none met the experts' standards.

[caption id="attachment_63664" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Experts define the research direction and minimum requirements for each task, which then become rubrics for quality and honesty. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Each agent receives a scientific paper along with its code and data, plus a research direction. Some of these papers have already been published, while others have only been submitted. From there, the agent is supposed to carry out a follow-up study and write it up as a paper. The 15 tasks come from ten researchers across quantum computing, plasma physics, chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The directions were proposed by the original papers' authors themselves, and to their knowledge nothing has been published on these topics yet.

[caption id="attachment_63666" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Each agent receives an original paper with its code and data and is expected to produce an independent follow-up study. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Open research poses a basic problem: there's no answer key. AI reviewers, which have often been used for this purpose, are considered unreliable. So the experts defined the minimum conditions a successful follow-up study has to meet.

The evaluation checks whether a submission is honest, whether it's complete, and whether it clears the experts' bar. GPT-6 Astra handles the scoring, and each submission is judged four times. The agents tested were Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. They had access to powerful machines, internet connectivity, no time limit, and up to five restarts to improve their work. In total, they ran for nearly 2,000 hours.

Only three agents produce honest work at all

Just three agents managed submissions without integrity violations: GPT-6 Astra on 11 of 15 tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol on six, and Claude Opus 5.5 on four. Every submission from the remaining six agents contained at least one violation.

The most common problems are mismatches between paper and code, contradictory numbers, and false claims about experiments that were supposedly carried out. Misreported baseline values pile up among the open models Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. Two submissions with hardcoded rather than computed results came from Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3.

[caption id="attachment_63667" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] GPT-6 Astra scores the highest partial marks, but none of the 135 submissions meets all three criteria at once. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Only one submission is complete, and it came from GPT-6 Astra. Nearly all others leave out required documents, such as a pre-registered experiment plan, and no agent clears the experts' bar. Under a more lenient scoring that accepts 90 percent of the rubric items, GPT-6 Astra comes closest, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol. The open models perform considerably worse overall.

[caption id="attachment_63670" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Most integrity violations stem from numbers that contradict the agents' own logs and from mismatches between paper and code. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

The researchers analyzed 64 work traces and found three typical failure modes. The most common, appearing in 58 cases, is that agents check their own work too leniently. In 34 cases, agents spot a problem but document it instead of fixing it. In 21 cases, they unilaterally shrink the scope of the task.

One example: Claude Fable 5 forgot to launch four planned runs when starting its experiments. Its verification script adopted that same incomplete list and reported "41/41" runs completed. The agent trusted that result until the very end. In a different task, GPT-5.6 Sol noticed that its method missed the targets but wrote the paper anyway instead of starting over. DeepSeek V4 Pro dropped experiments because they were supposedly too slow for the "remaining time budget," even though there was no time limit.

[caption id="attachment_63663" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] Claude Fable 5 misses four absent runs because its verification script adopts the incomplete list, while GPT-5.6 Sol writes the paper despite missing its targets. | Image: Kim et al[/caption]

There are counterexamples, too: in a quantum task, GPT-5.6 Sol caught a fundamental error, stopped the running experiments, and recomputed everything from scratch.

Longer runtimes didn't lead to better results. DeepSeek V4 Pro and GLM-5.3 ran the longest at median times of 19.5 and 13.9 hours but scored poorly. GPT-6 Astra got by with a median of just 1.3 hours and delivered the best results.

[caption id="attachment_42539" align="aligncenter" width="1800"] GPT-6 Astra has the shortest median runtime and delivers the best results. | Image: Kim et al.[/caption]

Because the strongest model also served as the evaluator, the researchers ran a cross-check: the original papers' authors judged anonymized AI papers themselves. On whether a paper matched the given research direction, the automated system agreed with the experts in every case.

Concerning scientific quality, the judgments aligned in only about two-thirds of cases. One expert criticized, for instance, that the papers didn't tell a story. Judgments like these remain the job of human reviewers, the authors say.

The study's code and data are publicly available, and the project page hosts a leaderboard of the tested models.

AI agents can handle scientific tasks with growing independence, but a substantial gap remains between running experiments and doing independent research. A study from August already showed how much AI agents struggle with unpublished research questions. Epoch AI and Anthropic recently found that agents tend to present their results too favorably and don't sufficiently question failed approaches.

The picture looks much better for well-defined tasks: GPT-6 Astra solved 49 out of 50 unpublished problems in theoretical physics, though those solutions could be verified unambiguously. An analysis of more than 700 tasks from AI development also showed that while agents take on more and more practical work, humans still make the key research decisions.

items.article_content_zh:
一项新的基准让人工智能代理致力于解决美国国家实验室的开放研究问题。特工们提交的论文看起来像是真正的研究，但往往声称他们的工作从未发生过。

人工智能代理能否独立回答尚未解决的研究问题？由卡内基梅隆大学研究人员领导的一个团队与美国能源部国家实验室的科学家合作，建立了一个名为“进入未知”的基准来找出答案。

根据该论文，当前 9 名 AI 代理提交的 135 份材料均未满足所有要求。作者将该基准视为系统地改进用于研究的人工智能代理的试验场，而不是质疑人工智能是否属于科学。

总共 114 份提交的内容已经未能通过完整性检查：大多数声称工作从未完成，或者引用了与自己的日志相矛盾的数字。作者写道，特工们很容易制作出看起来像是后续研究的文本，但没有一个符合专家的标准。

专家定义每项任务的研究方向和最低要求，然后这些成为质量和诚实的准则。 |图片：Kim 等人[/标题]

每个代理都会收到一篇科学论文及其代码和数据，以及一个研究方向。其中一些论文已经发表，而另一些则刚刚提交。从那里，代理应该进行后续研究并将其写成论文。这 15 项任务来自量子计算、等离子体物理、化学、材料科学和科学机器学习领域的 10 名研究人员。这些方向是由原始论文作者自己提出的，据他们所知，尚未就这些主题发表任何内容。

每个代理都会收到一份包含代码和数据的原始论文，并预计将产生独立的后续研究。 |图片：Kim 等人[/标题]

开放研究提出了一个基本问题：没有答案。经常用于此目的的人工智能评审员被认为是不可靠的。因此，专家们定义了成功的后续研究必须满足的最低条件。

评估会检查提交的内容是否诚实、是否完整以及是否通过了专家的审核。 GPT-6 Astra 负责评分，每份提交作品都会被评判四次。测试的代理包括 Claude Opus 4.8、Claude Opus 5、Claude Fable 5、Claude Opus 5.5、GPT-5.6 Sol、GPT-6 Astra、Deepseek V4 Pro、Kimi K3 和 GLM-5.3。他们可以使用功能强大的机器、互联网连接、没有时间限制，并且最多可以重新启动五次来改进他们的工作。他们总共运行了近 2,000 小时。

只有三个代理人能够诚实地工作

只有三个代理管理了没有完整性违规的提交：GPT-6 Astra 完成了 15 项任务中的 11 项，GPT-5.6 Sol 完成了 6 项任务，Claude Opus 5.5 完成了 4 项任务。其余六名特工提交的每份材料都至少包含一项违规行为。

最常见的问题是纸张和代码之间的不匹配、相互矛盾的数字以及对本应进行的实验的虚假陈述。开放模型 Deepseek V4 Pro、Kimi K3 和 GLM-5.3 中错误报告的基线值堆积如山。 Kimi K3 和 GLM-5.3 提交了两份具有硬编码结果而非计算结果的提交。

GPT-6 Astra 获得了最高的部分分数，但 135 份提交的作品中没有一个同时满足所有三个标准。 |图片：Kim 等人[/标题]

只有一份提交是完整的，它来自 GPT-6 Astra。几乎所有其他人都遗漏了所需的文件，例如预先注册的实验计划，并且没有代理人通过专家栏。在接受 90% 的评分标准的更宽松的评分下，GPT-6 Astra 最接近，其次是 Claude Opus 5.5 和 GPT-5.6 Sol。开放模型的整体表现要差得多。

items.title: Apps for Caregivers Get a Dose of AI, but That Might Not Be Enough
items.title_en: Apps for Caregivers Get a Dose of AI, but That Might Not Be Enough
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
We’re not alone in our struggles. According to AARP, in 2025, an estimated 63 million Americans cared for adults or children with a medical condition or disability. On average, these caregivers spend up to 27 hours per week providing care.

This caregiver crisis, where so many Americans provide ongoing, complex care and, as a result, endure poor health, financial strain, and isolation, is worsening as caregivers need more support and better systems.

Helpfully, to lighten the mental load, caregiver apps are aimed at families who are supporting seniors, children, or anyone with a diagnosis that needs regular management.

Every caregiver’s situation is different, and the apps and programs in this space reflect a diversity of needs.

Medisafe, which was created in 2013, tracks medications and sends reminders so users don’t miss a dose. The program can also notify a caregiver if a dose is missed. It gives its users the ability to track medical appointments, track their symptoms, and maintain a list of health care contacts and measurements. It also has a drug interaction checker where users can enter multiple medications to see if they are safe to take at the same time.

Caring Village, which was founded in 2015, has an appointment calendar, a to-do list, and a wellness journal where users can keep track of their loved one’s symptoms and moods, and even upload a photo. Caregivers can assign tasks through the app, create a care plan, and receive reminders to take medication. The app also comes with an AI assistant called Julia that can answer caregiving questions.

In 2022, Bret Koncak, based on his experiences with his two sons who have complex needs, cocreated Mejo, a web-based caregiver app. Users enter an individual’s medical history, which is then consolidated into a one-page summary that can be shared with caregivers, doctors, and therapists.

“A lot of people think that caregiving begins and ends with interactions with the health care system, but a lot of it is about what happens between care visits,” says Koncak. “That's what we're focused on.” For $6 a month or $60 a year, the premium version of Mejo gives users access to daily journaling, which they can share with other caregivers, so everyone stays on the same page without having to catch up verbally.

For now, information in Mejo is entered manually, but Koncak says his team is looking into ways to incorporate AI to help users come up with appropriate questions to ask during medical appointments.

Brett Rowell, whose son Briggs has cerebral palsy, is creating an app called Briggzy, so he and his wife, who work different hours, can more easily hand off their son’s care. Briggzy is currently in the testing phase, and Rowell hopes to launch it to a wider community in 2027.

“My wife took [our son] to most of the appointments because I worked 8 to 5 and she was off during that time,” said Rowell. “So the questionnaires alone, I don't know how to answer half of them unless I have Briggzy. My goal was to bring her mind into a shared space for me, so that way I can be helpful.”

Nasha Fitter, who has a daughter with a rare disease, launched Citizen Health in 2024 with cofounder Farid Vij to collect medical records for patients and store them in a secure portal. “With the users’ consent, we can extract information from those medical records, deidentify it, harmonize it, and start to pull an understanding of diseases through that,” says Fitter. “And then we feed that understanding back to patients so they would get a better sense of the trajectory of their child’s disease.” Citizen Health works with patient advocacy groups to support their research on drug development.

Six months ago, the company launched Ari, an AI “health teammate” that lets caregivers and patients track their loved one's care and symptoms by texting with it. Ari, currently in beta, can also access medical records, patient portals, and Google Calendar events, including specific appointment dates and surgeries. Ari notices caregiver patterns, such as whether they take medication at different times of the day and how that might impact symptoms. It prepares patients and caregivers for appointments by summarizing past medical information and providing appropriate questions to ask medical professionals. And it can help navigate insurance and government benefits.

Right now, Ari is only available for people with rare diseases, but the goal is to make it available and useful to all caregivers and patients.

I. Glenn Cohen, a bioethics and health law researcher and professor at Harvard Law School, is optimistic about AI in the health space overall. “For example, I think it will empower many patients to prep for questions they might want to ask their doctor before going in to see them.”

But he says that users should go into the process with their eyes open to understand the risks and what you're getting out of it, especially if a product is free or cheap.

Most of these devices are not medical devices, says Cohen. “As such, the FDA has not reviewed them, so their safety and efficacy remain a question mark, or it's the company's word for it that you have to take.”

The health information patients and caregivers plug into these AI tools is not protected by federal HIPAA statutes because the information is typically not coming from a covered entity. Instead, it comes from a person or from data collection at home. “If your privacy is important and you care about how the information is used, in some cases, all you can rely on is the contractual promises,” Cohen says. “They typically have language that absolves [the companies] from responsibility in many instances.”

He also warns that the information collected may not be only for the person receiving care, but may also include information about parents or other caregivers.

While I love the idea of keeping my son’s information all in one place so I can keep track of patterns, update his doctors without feeling emotionally drained, and easily hand off his caregiving needs to my husband, making sure we update the app regularly will be the key to actually seeing those benefits.

Denise M. Brown, CEO and founder of the Caregiving Years Training Academy, has seen many apps come and go because she says they can be tedious to maintain, especially when caregivers are already overloaded.

“We have to upload data to the app (care plans, schedules, tasks), and that’s a lot of work,” Brown says. “A physician, visiting nurse, therapist, or hospital discharge planner won’t log into the app to provide updates, which ends up falling back on the caregiver.”

At the end of the day, the need for caregiver apps is great, and many developers in this community, many of whom are caregivers themselves, are trying to do something to lessen the load.

“The technology and apps can open the door for broader seamless integration of care—and hopefully less stress on you as the caregiver,” says Nicole Howell, director of direct care workforce development at the National Council on Aging. But she says the final solution [to the overall caregiver crisis] will be something that not one family, not one caregiver can solve.

“It has to be all hands at the wheel. It has to be government. It has to be private. It has to be family members speaking up, saying the hard truth so we get the best of American ingenuity to move this to where we need to be.”

items.article_content_zh:
我们并不孤单地在挣扎。据 AARP 称，到 2025 年，估计有 6300 万美国人需要照顾患有疾病或残疾的成人或儿童。这些护理人员平均每周花费长达 27 个小时提供护理。

由于护理人员需要更多的支持和更好的系统，许多美国人提供持续、复杂的护理，因此面临健康状况不佳、经济紧张和孤立的情况，这场护理人员危机正在恶化。

有益的是，为了减轻精神负担，看护应用程序针对的是支持老年人、儿童或任何患有需要定期管理的诊断的人的家庭。

每个护理人员的情况都不同，这个领域的应用程序和程序反映了多样化的需求。

Medisafe 于 2013 年创建，可跟踪药物并发送提醒，以便用户不会错过服药。如果错过剂量，该程序还可以通知护理人员。它使用户能够跟踪医疗预约、跟踪他们的症状并维护医疗保健联系人和测量结果的列表。它还具有药物相互作用检查器，用户可以输入多种药物，看看同时服用它们是否安全。

Caring Village 成立于 2015 年，提供预约日历、待办事项列表和健康日记，用户可以在其中跟踪亲人的症状和情绪，甚至上传照片。护理人员可以通过应用程序分配任务、制定护理计划并接收服药提醒。该应用程序还配备了一个名为 Julia 的人工智能助手，可以回答护理问题。

2022 年，Bret Koncak 根据他与两个有着复杂需求的儿子的经历，共同创建了 Mejo，一款基于网络的护理应用程序。用户输入个人的病史，然后将其合并为一页摘要，可以与护理人员、医生和治疗师共享。

“很多人认为护理的开始和结束都是与医疗保健系统的互动，但其中很多是关于护理访问之间发生的事情，”Koncak 说。 “这就是我们关注的重点。”每月 6 美元或每年 60 美元，Mejo 的高级版本让用户可以访问每日日记，他们可以与其他护理人员分享这些日记，这样每个人都可以保持在同一页面上，而无需口头交流。

目前，Mejo 中的信息是手动输入的，但 Koncak 表示，他的团队正在研究如何整合人工智能，以帮助用户在医疗预约期间提出适当的问题。

Brett Rowell 的儿子 Briggs 患有脑瘫，他正在开发一款名为 Briggzy 的应用程序，这样他和工作时间不同的妻子就可以更轻松地照顾儿子。 Briggzy 目前正处于测试阶段，Rowell 希望在 2027 年将其推出到更广泛的社区。

“我的妻子带着（我们的儿子）参加了大部分的预约，因为我朝八晚五工作，而她在那段时间休息，”罗威尔说。 “仅凭问卷调查，除非有 Briggzy，否则我不知道如何回答其中一半问题。我的目标是让她的思想与我共享空间，这样我就能提供帮助。”

Nasha Fitter 的女儿患有罕见疾病，她与联合创始人 Farid Vij 于 2024 年推出了 Citizen Health，收集患者的医疗记录并将其存储在安全门户中。 “在用户同意的情况下，我们可以从这些医疗记录中提取信息，对其进行去识别化、协调化，并开始通过这些信息了解疾病，”菲特说。 “然后我们将这种理解反馈给患者，以便他们更好地了解孩子的疾病轨迹。” Citizen Health 与患者倡导团体合作，支持他们的药物开发研究。

六个月前，该公司推出了人工智能“健康队友”Ari，让护理人员和患者可以通过发短信来跟踪亲人的护理和症状。目前处于测试阶段的 Ari 还可以访问医疗记录、患者门户和 Google 日历事件，包括特定的预约日期和手术。阿里注意到护理人员的模式，例如他们是否在一天的不同时间服药以及这可能如何影响症状。它通过总结过去的医疗信息并提供适当的问题来询问医疗专业人员，为患者和护理人员的预约做好准备。它还可以帮助了解保险和政府福利。

目前，Ari 仅适用于患有罕见疾病的人，但目标是使其对所有护理人员和患者都可用且有用。

items.title: Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff
items.title_en: Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
A Google Research AI can detect signs of high blood pressure using a regular smartwatch, with no blood pressure cuff needed for calibration. The AI relies on two sensors already built into modern watches—a pulse sensor and a motion sensor—according to a Google blog post. The study was published in Nature.

A neural network learned from nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data by comparing short segments and figuring out which ones belonged to the same person, picking up typical pulse and heartbeat patterns without any diagnoses to guide it. The system then averages these patterns over several days and calculates a probability for high blood pressure. Google's health model SensorFM also learns from smartwatch data.

In a study of 196 people across five US research sites, the watch spotted hypertension about as well as a traditional cuff, identifying 65.8 percent of those with high blood pressure compared to 55.3 percent for the standard in-office measurement.

Google says the findings have been folded into the blood pressure trends feature in the Google Health app, but the method is still a research project and doesn't replace a diagnosis. The goal is to nudge people toward getting checked. More than half of people with high blood pressure don't know they have it, according to Google.

items.article_content_zh:
谷歌研究人工智能可以使用普通智能手表检测高血压迹象，无需血压袖带进行校准。根据谷歌博客文章，人工智能依赖于现代手表中内置的两个传感器——脉冲传感器和运动传感器。该研究发表在《自然》杂志上。

神经网络通过比较短片段并找出哪些片段属于同一个人，从近 500,000 小时的传感器数据中学习，在没有任何诊断指导的情况下获取典型的脉搏和心跳模式。然后，系统对几天内的这些模式进行平均，并计算出高血压的概率。谷歌的健康模型 SensorFM 也可以从智能手表数据中学习。

在一项针对美国 5 个研究中心 196 人的研究中，这款手表发现高血压的效果与传统袖带的效果相当，识别出 65.8% 的高血压患者，而标准办公室测量的识别率为 55.3%。

谷歌表示，这些发现已被纳入谷歌健康应用程序的血压趋势功能中，但该方法仍然是一个研究项目，并不能取代诊断。目标是促使人们接受检查。据谷歌称，超过一半的高血压患者并不知道自己患有高血压。

items.title: OpenAI lands an $11 billion funding round, but has to court dentists for more capital
items.title_en: OpenAI lands an $11 billion funding round, but has to court dentists for more capital
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
OpenAI has received roughly $11 billion in new funding, the first tranche of a round valuing the company at $1.25 trillion. The money was wired on Friday, Bloomberg reports. The full round could grow to $20 billion, with the rest expected in the coming weeks. OpenAI originally sought $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation but scaled back after an AI-sector selloff. Anthropic's valuation is also under pressure ahead of its planned IPO.

Investors include Coatue Management, T. Rowe Price, SoftBank, Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund, Andreessen Horowitz, and a consortium from the United Arab Emirates. OpenAI is also working with investment banks to bring in wealthy individual investors. If OpenAI is already courting dentists to scrape together more capital, it tells you the AI funding market is either tapped out or too concentrated on OpenAI and Anthropic. Anthropic's massive B2B success with Claude Code is making life even harder for OpenAI.

OpenAI 已获得约 110 亿美元的新融资，这是该公司估值 1.25 万亿美元的第一轮融资。据彭博社报道，这笔钱已于周五汇出。整轮融资可能会增至 200 亿美元，其余预计将在未来几周内完成。 OpenAI 最初以 1.4 万亿美元的估值寻求 300 亿美元的融资，但在人工智能行业遭遇抛售后缩减了规模。在计划首次公开募股之前，Anthropic 的估值也面临压力。

投资者包括 Coatue Management、T. Rowe Price、软银、红杉资本、Founders Fund、Andreessen Horowitz 以及来自阿拉伯联合酋长国的财团。 OpenAI 还与投资银行合作，引进富有的个人投资者。如果 OpenAI 已经在吸引牙医筹集更多资金，那么这说明人工智能融资市场要么已经被耗尽，要么过于集中于 OpenAI 和 Anthropic。 Anthropic 凭借 Claude Code 在 B2B 领域取得的巨大成功让 OpenAI 的日子变得更加艰难。

items.title: Global tablet shipments fell 23% YoY to 32M units in Q3 2026, their lowest level in nearly three years; Apple's iPad shipments fell 27.5% YoY to ~11.58M (Omdia)
items.title_en: Global tablet shipments fell 23% YoY to 32M units in Q3 2026, their lowest level in nearly three years; Apple's iPad shipments fell 27.5% YoY to ~11.58M (Omdia)
items.author: Omdia
items.article_content:
LONDON, November 5, 2026: The global tablet market fell 23% year-over-year (YoY) to 32 million units in Q3 2026, marking its lowest shipment level in nearly three years, according to Omdia’s latest research. The Middle East, China and Western Europe were the hardest-hit regions, experiencing sharper declines than the rest of the market.

"Following a 10% decline last quarter, the tablet market recorded another double-digit contraction in Q3," said Himani Mukka, Research Manager at Omdia. "As supply constraints intensify, tablets are increasingly taking a backseat in vendors' strategic priorities for 2026 and 2027. With supply conditions expected to tighten further next year, a meaningful recovery in the tablet market is unlikely before 2028.”

In 3Q26, Apple maintained its lead despite a 28% YoY decline in shipments. Its market share fell to 36% from 38.2% a year earlier, as its shipments declined more sharply than the overall market.

Samsung remained in second place, shipping 5.4 million units, down 22 % YoY, and capturing a 16.9% market share. Despite new tablet launches, the company continued to face pressure as component constraints weighed on shipment volumes.

As in Q2, Lenovo was the only top-five vendor to post growth, with shipments increasing 12% YoY to 4.1 million units. Its market share climbed to 12.7%, up from 8.7% a year earlier, marking the largest share increase among vendors this quarter. While detachable shipments declined sharply year on year, slate tablets drove overall growth, supported by stronger sell-in across all regions except Europe and Latin America.

Xiaomi ranked fourth, shipping 2.3 million tablets, down 11% year on year. Its market share rose modestly to 7.3%, supported by a strong quarter in Latin America. Huawei rounded out the top five with 1.8 million units, recording the steepest decline among the leading vendors at 43% year on year. Despite the overall downturn, the vendor continued to register growth in CEE and APAC this quarter.

Mukka added,“We have seen several major tablet launches in the back half of the year, including Samsung's flagship Galaxy Tab S12 series, Apple's OLED-equipped iPad mini, and Xiaomi's Pad 9 series. Huawei, HONOR, OnePlus and realme have also introduced new models recently. However, these launches have done little to stimulate consumer demand amid challenging market conditions.”

“Persistent supply constraints are also limiting vendors' ability to deliver meaningful specification upgrades, leaving fewer compelling differences between new models and their predecessors. As a result, consumers are increasingly expected to delay purchases until more substantial improvements become available.”

items.article_content_zh:
伦敦，2026 年 11 月 5 日：根据 Omdia 的最新研究，2026 年第三季度全球平板电脑市场同比下降 23%，至 3200 万台，创下近三年来的最低出货量。中东、中国和西欧是受灾最严重的地区，其跌幅比市场其他地区更严重。

Omdia 研究经理 Himani Mukka 表示：“继上季度下滑 10% 后，平板电脑市场在第三季度再次出现两位数萎缩。” “随着供应限制的加剧，平板电脑在供应商 2026 年和 2027 年的战略重点中日益退居次席。由于明年供应状况预计将进一步收紧，平板电脑市场在 2028 年之前不太可能出现有意义的复苏。”

26 年第三季度，尽管苹果出货量同比下降 28%，但仍保持领先地位。由于出货量下降幅度超过整体市场，其市场份额从去年同期的 38.2% 下降至 36%。

三星仍位居第二，出货量为 540 万台，同比下降 22%，占据 16.9% 的市场份额。尽管推出了新的平板电脑，但由于组件限制影响了出货量，该公司继续面临压力。

与第二季度一样，联想是前五名中唯一实现增长的厂商，出货量同比增长 12% 至 410 万台。其市场份额从去年同期的8.7%攀升至12.7%，是本季度厂商中份额增幅最大的。尽管可拆卸出货量同比大幅下降，但在除欧洲和拉丁美洲以外的所有地区销售强劲的支撑下，平板电脑推动了整体增长。

小米排名第四，平板电脑出货量为230万台，同比下降11%。在拉丁美洲强劲季度的支撑下，其市场份额小幅上升至 7.3%。华为以 180 万台跻身前五，同比下降 43%，是领先厂商中跌幅最大的。尽管整体低迷，该供应商本季度在中东欧和亚太地区继续实现增长。

Mukka补充道：“今年下半年，我们看到了几款主要的平板电脑发布，包括三星旗舰产品Galaxy Tab S12系列、苹果配备OLED的iPad mini和小米Pad 9系列。华为、荣耀、一加和realme最近也推出了新机型。然而，在充满挑战的市场条件下，这些发布对刺激消费者需求作用甚微。”

“持续的供应限制也限制了供应商提供有意义的规格升级的能力，从而使新型号与其前身之间的显着差异减少。因此，越来越多的消费者预计会推迟购买，直到出现更多实质性改进。”

items.content_snippet: Shenzhen clears out illicit markets for smuggled chips and stolen iPhones as it prepares to host gathering of international leaders
items.summary_en: Shenzhen is clearing out illicit electronics markets like Huaqiangbei, specifically targeting the smuggling of chips and stolen iPhone trade. The action aims to clean up the industry environment ahead of the upcoming APEC summit.
items.title_zh: 深圳清理电子黑市迎峰会
items.summary_zh: 深圳在APEC峰会前夕整顿华强北等电子市场，重点打击芯片走私及翻新机交易，规范电子产业链环境

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 深圳近日对华强北等电子产品聚集区展开清理行动，针对非法芯片贸易与盗窃翻新手机市场进行打击。此举旨在改善国际峰会前的城市形象与行业秩序，试图将野蛮生长的灰色产业纳入监管视线。

items.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
items.title_en: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

OpenAI 在新一轮融资中目前估值为 1.25 万亿美元，该轮融资又筹集了 110 亿美元。这将使其成为世界上最有价值的公司之一，不久之后，该公司于 3 月份以 8520 亿美元的估值从投资者那里筹集了 1220 亿美元。

彭博社回应《金融时报》和《华尔街日报》上周的报道称，OpenAI 仍在寻求额外投资，可能将融资金额增加至 200 亿美元，并且最初希望以 1.4 万亿美元的估值筹集至多 300 亿美元。那是在科技股下跌之前，中期选举的结果表明公众舆论已经转向反对人工智能公司和数据中心项目。

OpenAI 的竞争对手 Anthropic 上周提交了 S-1 上市申请。今年早些时候，OpenAI 首席执行官 Sam Altman 表示，公司将推迟 IPO，直到对其模型的安全性做出更有信心的声明。他没有给出 IPO 的具体时间表，但当时表示，“我认为，如果 OpenAI 等待太久才上市，对世界来说也是件坏事。”

items.title_zh: 苹果称iPhone Duo专用应用已破十万大关
items.summary_zh: 苹果宣布专为iPhone Duo设计的应用已超10万款，且每日新增数千款优化应用

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 苹果官方近期宣布，针对iPhone Duo开发的专用App Store应用数量已正式突破10万大关，并保持着每天数千款的增长速度。尽管已进行大规模适配，部分应用在双屏交互下的用户体验仍有待优化。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Apple officially announced that the App Store now features over 100,000 apps specifically designed for the iPhone Duo, with thousands more added daily. Despite the rapid growth in optimized software, user experience for some apps on the dual-screen form factor remains a work in progress.

elements_zh.what: 专用适配应用突破10万，并维持高速增长
elements_zh.why: 推动iPhone Duo双屏硬件的普及与生态适配

elements_en.what: Reached 100k+ dedicated apps with rapid daily additions

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 应用数量虽多，但这种为了填补屏幕缝隙而强行适配的操作，本质上还是在考验开发者“缝合”代码的耐心。毕竟用户买的是创新，不是一个比原来多装了十万个图标的折叠屏充电宝。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Hitting 100k apps is just a numbers game for PR; most users just want a seamless experience, not a glorified charging brick with a thousand redundant icons. It’s a classic case of 'if you build it, they will come'—eventually, maybe.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌正式收购了Crusoe位于怀俄明州东南部的土地资产。这一地块原为Crusoe筹建的数据中心项目，但由于该项目未能成功争取到谷歌等关键客户入驻，最终沦为被金主爸爸“反向收购”的资产。

elements_en.what: Google bought out Crusoe's data center site

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 创业公司想靠建数据中心“空手套大厂”确实不容易，最后没能把云服务卖给谷歌，干脆把自己打包卖给谷歌了。这哪是商业合作，分明是一场“乙方变废纸、甲方直接收尸”的精准降维打击。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Attempting to trap big tech in a data center deal is a bold move that backfired spectacularly; when you can't sell them the cloud, you end up selling them your empty dirt. It’s a brutal reminder that in the AI arms race, if you aren't the landlord, you're just the furniture.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌旗下风投机构近期购入约300万股高通股票，交易总金额约5.48亿美元。此举意在强化双方在数据中心芯片领域的战略协同，试图在高算力竞赛中绕开单一供应商的桎梏。

items.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
items.title_en: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
items.author: Ars Technica
items.article_content:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security.

The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.

Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It's not clear why the company considered such

items.title: All the latest updates on AI data centers
items.title_en: All the latest updates on AI data centers
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
Massive new data centers are the physical foundation for tech companies’ hopes and dreams for AI. But the rush to expand warehouses full of energy-hungry servers has also kicked up fights across the world over their impact on power grids, utility bills, nearby communities, and the environment.

Data centers were a major bipartisan issue ahead of the 2026 midterms, and voters largely opposed data center expansion at the polls. Tech giants like OpenAI and Amazon are promising to work more closely with local communities and cover their data center energy costs. But following the election, Democratic leaders are calling for further data center restrictions and slowdowns that the AI companies will have to grapple with.

From audacious plans about data centers into space, heated local battles over buildouts, and potential environmental impacts, here’s The Verge’s news, coverage, and reporting surrounding data centers and the companies that are building them.

items.title: Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong agentic coding results as a fully Apache 2.0 open US model
items.title_en: Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong agentic coding results as a fully Apache 2.0 open US model
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Ricursive Intelligence is releasing Ripple-65B Preview, a 65-billion-parameter open-weight language model that the company says achieves the top score among open-source U.S. models on the TerminalBench 2.1 coding benchmark at a total R&D cost of $32 million. On other benchmarks, however, Ripple falls behind the likewise newly released western open model Inkling 2 Small.

The article Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong agentic coding results as a fully Apache 2.0 open US model appeared first on The Decoder.

items.title: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking
items.title_en: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities, set out to test how well different AI models could carry out complex, multi-step network instructions on mock corporate networks.

“The best frontier models, locked up inside the labs and available only through trusted access programs, are now starting to be matched by open models that anybody can download,” says Nikil Ravi, a researcher at Vals.

The company’s findings suggest that closed models no longer have a definitive edge in cyber skills, meaning recent efforts by frontier labs to limit access to their models, and thereby slow the proliferation of such capabilities, may potentially be moot.

The findings are also noteworthy given that the US frontier labs, particularly Anthropic, premised the limited release of new models—beginning with Claude Mythos Preview in April—on the idea that gated access would only buy time before advanced hacking capabilities were broadly available.

Anthropic's frontier red team lead, Logan Graham, told WIRED in April that the company’s Project Glasswing, which gives trusted access to the full capabilities of new models, was focused on getting those tools “in the hands of defenders to give a head start.”

“We need to prepare now for a world where these capabilities are broadly available in 6, 12, 24 months. Many things would be different about security,” he told WIRED at the time.

Seven months later, that transition seems to have arrived on schedule.

Vals tested AI models in two simulated scenarios, giving them various specific tasks to achieve. The first scenario involved a mock corporate network accessible through a public-facing website. The second involved two different company networks; a model needed to compromise the first in order to gain access to the second.

The researchers found OpenAI’s most advanced cyber model, Daybreak, which is available only to trusted partners, to be the most capable, completing 81 percent of the tasks it was given in an average of two tests. The Chinese open-weight model DeepSeek was not far behind, completing 73 percent of the objectives on average. The Vals researchers note that on some tasks, the two models scored equally.

The research also showed how much cheaper it is to use an open-weight model for this kind of task. Vals says it costs $17 to $46 in tokens for GPT-6-Sol to carry out an attack compared to $2 to $3 for DeepSeek. Open models are generally cheaper because they can be run on one’s own hardware. Rayan Krishnan, CEO of Vals, says this also provides a strong incentive for those playing defense to use open models rather than proprietary ones.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Much of the year in cybersecurity has played out as predicted, with AI automating core hacking tasks to help both attackers and defenders find a massive number of new vulnerabilities in code and rapidly probe networks for weaknesses. While the speed and scale of the findings, and the intensity of fixing uncovered software flaws, have all increased, experts are still debating whether AI has fundamentally altered the conceptual foundation and tenets of cybersecurity defense. In other words, it’s still not clear whether AI tools pose a new kind of threat or amplify the security challenges that have long existed.

The fact that open-weight models are now starting to match closed ones is crucial for understanding how criminal hackers can harness AI, and how companies and developers should respond. But in practice, real-world observation of cybercriminal and state-backed hacking activity has repeatedly shown in recent months that attackers are doing what they always do by conserving their resources and generally making do with older and less capable models—both proprietary and open—for most of their activity. And even with strict controls, defenders must assume that the best-funded and most highly motivated attackers have already had at least some access to closed models all this time.

“I am in general agreement that open-weight models are capable of producing advanced attacks and vulnerabilities today, especially when you consider the abliterated models that disable safety training by modifying weights,” says Alex Zenla, cofounder and chief technology officer of the cloud security firm Edera. “My caveat to this is that it is likely that the closed labs have trained additional, unreleased models exceeding these capabilities. So I would put this very much like a cat-and-mouse game. The labs see themselves as moving fast to outpace the open-weight models, to be able to secure vulnerabilities before the open-weight models find them. Unfortunately, I do think this may be the beginning of a dangerous security landscape.”

items.article_content_zh:
Vals 是一家测量人工智能能力的公司，它开始测试不同的人工智能模型在模拟企业网络上执行复杂的多步骤网络指令的效果。

瓦尔斯研究员尼基尔·拉维 (Nikil Ravi) 表示：“最好的前沿模型被锁在实验室内，只能通过可信访问程序获得，现在开始与任何人都可以下载的开放模型相匹配。”

该公司的研究结果表明，封闭模型在网络技能方面不再具有明确的优势，这意味着前沿实验室最近限制对其模型的访问，从而减缓此类能力扩散的努力可能没有实际意义。

鉴于美国前沿实验室（尤其是 Anthropic）以​​有限发布新模型（从 4 月份的 Claude Mythos 预览版开始）为前提，这一发现也值得注意，因为门控访问只会在高级黑客功能广泛可用之前赢得时间。

Anthropic 的前沿红队负责人 Logan Graham 在 4 月份告诉《连线》杂志，该公司的 Glasswing 项目提供了对新模型全部功能的可信访问，其重点是让这些工具“交到防御者手中，以取得领先优势”。

“我们现在需要做好准备，迎接这些功能在 6、12、24 个月内广泛可用的世界。安全方面的许多事情都会有所不同，”他当时告诉《连线》杂志。

七个月后，这一转变似乎已如期到来。

瓦尔斯在两个模拟场景中测试了人工智能模型，赋予它们要完成的各种特定任务。第一个场景涉及通过面向公众的网站访问的模拟公司网络。第二个涉及两个不同的公司网络；模型需要妥协第一个才能获得第二个。

研究人员发现 OpenAI 最先进的网络模型 Daybreak 能力最强，平均在两次测试中完成了 81% 的任务，该模型仅提供给值得信赖的合作伙伴。中国的开放权重模型 DeepSeek 也不甘落后，平均完成了 73% 的目标。瓦尔斯研究人员指出，在某些任务上，这两个模型得分相同。

该研究还表明，使用开放权重模型来完成此类任务要便宜得多。 Vals 表示，GPT-6-Sol 进行攻击的代币成本为 17 至 46 美元，而 DeepSeek 的代币成本为 2 至 3 美元。开放模型通常更便宜，因为它们可以在自己的硬件上运行。 Vals 首席执行官 Rayan Krishnan 表示，这也为那些从事防御工作的人提供了强有力的激励，让他们使用开放模型而不是专有模型。

OpenAI 没有立即回应置评请求。

今年的网络安全大部分时间都按照预期进行，人工智能自动化核心黑客任务，帮助攻击者和防御者发现代码中的大量新漏洞，并快速探测网络的弱点。尽管调查结果的速度和规模以及修复已发现的软件缺陷的强度都在增加，但专家们仍在争论人工智能是否从根本上改变了网络安全防御的概念基础和原则。换句话说，目前尚不清楚人工智能工具是否会带来新的威胁，或者会加剧长期存在的安全挑战。

事实上，开放权重模型现在开始与封闭式模型相匹配，这一事实对于理解犯罪黑客如何利用人工智能以及公司和开发人员应如何应对至关重要。但在实践中，近几个月来对网络犯罪和国家支持的黑客活动的现实观察一再表明，攻击者正在做他们一贯做的事情，即节省资源，并且通常在大部分活动中使用旧的和能力较差的模型（专有的和开放的）。即使有严格的控制，防御者也必须假设资金最充足、积极性最高的攻击者一直以来至少已经拥有对封闭模型的部分访问权限。

云安全公司 Edera 联合创始人兼首席技术官 Alex Zenla 表示：“我普遍认为开放权重模型如今能够产生高级攻击和漏洞，特别是当你考虑到通过修改权重来禁用安全训练的废除模型时。” “我对此的警告是，封闭实验室很可能已经训练了超过这些能力的额外的、未发布的模型。因此，我认为这非常像猫捉老鼠的游戏。实验室认为自己正在快速超越开放权重模型，以便能够在开放权重模型发现漏洞之前保护漏洞。不幸的是，我确实认为这可能是危险安全格局的开始。”

items.title: Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
items.title_en: Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

You can create things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, or music tracker directly within Muse.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within Muse. The new feature, called “spaces,” allows its AI assistant to build things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker, trivia game, and more, which you can interact with directly in the Muse app.

Meta says you can create a new space by describing it. If you connect an outside app to Muse — like Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, Notion, and others Muse works with — the AI assistant will continuously pull information from them, allowing it to update pricing, dates, and other information in your space in the background. You can also interact with elements inside your spaces by checking things off, adding notes, and making edits.

You can also change the placement of your spaces in the Muse app, too, as Meta lets you keep them in the sidebar, move them into your main tab, or schedule when you see them. “For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday,” Meta says.

Meta also announced that it’s bringing new “Active Memory” and “Active Focus” capabilities from its Muse Wonder AI model into the Muse app and its Meta AI chatbot. This will allow Muse to understand when past information becomes relevant during conversations, as well as make it better at working toward goals.

Meta is rolling out spaces to all Muse users. The company is also looking into ways to share your spaces with other users and collaborate with them.

items.title: AI is the new dating dealbreaker
items.title_en: AI is the new dating dealbreaker
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When Irene moved to San Francisco last year, she started using dating apps as a way to meet new people, get to know her new city, and connect with others who care about the things she does. After the 25-year-old analyst downloaded Hinge and started swiping, she noticed a trend.

“Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if”,” she recalls. “Sometimes people will be like, ‘Fuck AI.’”

Usually, the people who include this kind of value statement on their profile work in the arts, nursing, maybe graphic design. Within the span of a few minutes of sitting down and swiping, Irene shows me a second profile where this happened once more: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.”

In San Francisco, the epicenter of tech, the metaphorical AI bomb went off in 2022 with the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Conversations surrounding artificial intelligence now permeate the dating scene in one shape or another. Over the past month, I bopped around the city, chatting with people at parties and coworking spaces and reviewing dating directories and other online profiles, trying to find out how AI affects the dating scene.

Responses varied wildly. For some, AI feelings take on a similar valence to traditionally political ones, showing up in dating profiles next to party affiliation or other signifiers, like the watermelon emoji symbolizing solidarity with Palestinians amid the war in Gaza. Others are wrestling with the ethics of dating someone who builds AI, considering the financial benefits a partner in the industry can bring, weighing whether to have children in a future this uncertain, or even handing their love lives over to it entirely.

On a street near Berkeley, I meet up with Kyle. (His name has been changed so that he can talk openly about his personal life.) Kyle is a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit initiative, and although he is just in his early 20s, he’s already thinking about death. In the AI safety community, some experts see a 10 percent chance of humans going extinct due to AI taking over. This apocalyptic possibility is always top of mind when he navigates conversations with a potential partner: The rapid development of AI shapes how he thinks about whether he wants to have kids or where he might live long term — if there is even a long term.

“It’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future.”

“A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years down the line,” Kyle says, raising his gaze and looking off into the distance. Life could change depending on whether the world manages to get AI alignment right, he tells me. “For me, it’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future,” he says. He tries to have these conversations in person rather than over text, so a date can ask follow-up questions about why he sees the future the way he does.

For now, he’s focusing on finding a partner with whom he enjoys spending time.

When I ask Kyle if he would date someone who works in artificial intelligence or tech, he says that he would have to think hard about it. He believes that a lot of people who work at frontier AI companies are doing things that he considers pretty heinous. “They don’t think very hard about the societal impacts of their actions because they’re mostly in it for the paycheck or because it’s interesting,” he says.

But Bryan, who works at a frontier AI company and also asked to go by a pseudonym, doesn’t believe that feelings about AI matter when it comes to romance.

“I just don’t think it’s a factor at all. Like, it’s the least [relevant] thing,” says Bryan, who recently started a relationship. To him, dating is more about weighing a series of factors: how someone talks and approaches problems, how they have fun. Despite his day job (and whatever someone like Kyle might think of him for it), he believes that working out more and looking better probably increases someone’s chances of getting a match way more than any AI or non-AI affiliation. But, he says, “The one way it interacts is that there are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.”

Bryan isn’t exactly wrong about the benefits of a high-paying job in AI. With the IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI in the next year, matchmakers have found that clients are specifying “AI engineer” on their list of preferred dating profile qualifications. And stability is particularly attractive right now: According to a CBRE report released in August, more than 20,000 AI jobs were added to the San Francisco Bay Area’s technology workforce, even as overall tech talent contracted by 6 percent since 2022. “Member of technical staff” roles have become very lucrative jobs; the average salary of an AI researcher can be around $300,000. According to the New York Post, one matchmaker found that her client booked a six-month stay in San Francisco because of the possibility of meeting a significant other who might be connected to an AI company going through an IPO.

AI is reflected in the way the technology is seeping into San Franciscans’ everyday habits — including those that shape relationships, from how people process their feelings to whom they confide in.

Andromeda, who works as an EMT and a registered behavior technician as well as an AI security analyst, says she’s worried about the unintended consequences of talking to AI chatbots, especially for questions about (and possibly the replacement of) human connection. According to a study released by Elon University, 27 percent of Americans are turning to AI chatbots with personal, emotional, or social queries. Thirty-eight percent of the surveyed group said they occasionally tell AI things that they would not tell other people, including their romantic partners. Andromeda weighs the pros and cons of dating someone who would use bots for “emotional regulation.”

“Socially and psychologically, it’s a big deal, and we have to talk about it,” she says. She appreciates the role that a chatbot can play to help someone better express themselves. “I would certainly date a man who uses AI to talk through intense thoughts and feelings and to brainstorm clarity.”

At the same time, she is also reluctant to date someone who might abuse a chatbot, since it’s maladaptive behavior and does not represent good values for model welfare. “If they treat ChatGPT badly today, it will be me tomorrow!”

“There are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.”

If Andromeda worries about what people tell chatbots, others have gone a step further and let AI do the talking for them.

At the Hugging Face Open Source Week party, Joseph, a 21-year-old software engineer, explains how he has automated his dating life. Working 14 hours a day to launch his startup, he has decided to outsource swiping on Hinge entirely to an AI agent. The agent is managed by his human virtual assistant from the Philippines and has been fine-tuned to mimic the way that he speaks and acts. Looking at each profile, the AI agent sends tailored outreach messages to spark a conversation. After some back and forth, the agent determines if the woman is compatible with Joseph and, if so, books open slots on his weekend calendars for dating in person.

“If you are a founder, you have to put a value on your time, so you can’t be doing low-leverage activities. Protect your dopamine, folks,” Joseph tells me at The Midway in San Francisco’s Dogpatch district, where hundreds don white bucket hats and dance next to Hugging Face’s round, foam emoji mascot. “It’s kind of a copy-and-paste sequence that happens with every girl to get to know about you, understand your backstory, and so on and so forth.”

He’s not alone. A 2025 survey by Match and the Kinsey Institute found that 26 percent of singles in the United States use AI tools to enhance their dating experiences. Hinge now has an AI tool to generate suggested responses and Bumble, which will soon phase out swiping, has launched Bee, an AI assistant-facilitated matchmaking tool. (Bumble VP of Communications Natalie Logan said in an email that Bumble has not yet announced the update to the swipe, and that Bee operates independently of that update.)

“It has been extremely successful. I’m averaging two closed conversions a week,” he says, meaning that he goes on two dates with two different people. The women on the other side don’t know. The point is to meet in real life. The overall process has lowered what he calls “CPN,” or “cost per nut.”

At 29 years old, JJ has stopped using dating apps. Instead, she turns to the Date-Me Directory — a collection of longform, resume-like documents where people write personal dating profiles — to find a partner. Two years ago, she worked in product design in New York, but she transitioned into the AI safety field because she felt that it aligned more with her effective altruist morals.

Upon reviewing troves of Date-Me Docs for the San Francisco / Berkeley area, I noticed that quite a few people mention “the singularity” as a factor of whether to have kids. The so-called “singularity” is the point of when technology overtakes human control; some have pointed to the development of true artificial general intelligence as the point of no return. According to JJ, many people in AI safety specifically use the Date-Me Docs as a way to meet people.

“Don’t want kids in the pre-singularity future, if there’s a post-singularity future then I might want kids then,” one document states.

On the other hand, similar to climate doom anxieties, other people are looking at whether having children is ethical amid massive structural changes in society caused by AI.

“Is the world good, getting to a good place, or is it bad? And if it’s good, baby. If not, no baby, because you’re gonna bring a baby into a world full of potential suffering,” JJ says, explaining the train of thought that these Date-Me Doc potential suitors might have. She does not consider herself a doomer, but she is still pressed for her own singularity timeline. (2029, she suspects.) If anything, she jokes that the approaching end times makes her more likely to want a baby around: “If the bomb gets me, I want to be holding a shiny child.”

These existential concerns have translated into a backlash against tech, San Francisco included. “Stop the AI” rallies have spread to events like Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention and OpenAI’s DevDay, with protestors calling out tech companies and their roles in data center development and ICE raids.

“If there’s a post-singularity future then I might want kids then.”

That skepticism has spilled into how people size up a potential match, even at local events designed to bring the Bay Area together. At a pop-up “Date My Friend” pitch event at the Kilowatt Bar in the Mission District on a Saturday evening, a dozen people pitched their friends and exes to a crowd of more than a hundred.

“He works in tech, but he’s unhappy about it,” one person announced to a chorus of cheers. Other people cracked jokes that their PowerPoints were clearly made by humans, not AI.

Annalise Wulf, 26, one of the three cofounders of the “Date My Friend” series, says that although people in San Francisco try to “tech maxx” their lives, more tech workers with crazy schedules are interested in analog, in-person events to go back to the roots of meeting and creating community. “It’s like, ‘I’m here because I’m not using an AI dating app right now. Like I’m trying to do something different,’” Wulf says.

“I do think it’s maybe popular now to be more anti-tech,” says Lucy Segraves, 28, one of the other cofounders. If someone is working for a company that people see as perpetuating war crimes through their technology, she might be more hesitant to date them.

But ultimately, she says, there are more immediate concerns. “As a person with a non-tech job, I never judge someone if they do work in tech,” Lucy says. “Because that’s unfortunately where the money is, and we’re all just trying to make it in life.”

Update, November 6th, 2026: This story has been updated to clarify the relationship between Bumble’s future plans to eliminate the swipe and it’s new AI matchmaking tool.

当艾琳去年搬到旧金山时，她开始使用约会应用程序来结识新朋友，了解她的新城市，并与关心她所做的事情的其他人建立联系。这位 25 岁的分析师下载 Hinge 并开始刷卡后，她注意到了一个趋势。

“Hinge 有一个提示，你可以说，‘我们会相处得很好，如果’，”她回忆道，“有时人们会说，‘去他妈的人工智能。’”

通常，在个人资料中包含这种价值观的人从事艺术、护理工作，也许还从事平面设计工作。在坐下来刷卡的几分钟内，艾琳向我展示了第二个个人资料，这种情况再次发生：“如果……你使用人工智能，你不应该和我出去。”

在科技中心旧金山，随着 OpenAI 的 ChatGPT 的发布，隐喻的人工智能炸弹于 2022 年引爆。围绕人工智能的对话现在以这样或那样的形式渗透到约会场景中。在过去的一个月里，我在城市里闲逛，在聚会和联合办公空间与人们聊天，查看约会目录和其他在线资料，试图找出人工智能如何影响约会场景。

反应差异很大。对于一些人来说，人工智能的情感与传统的政治情感有着相似的价值，出现在约会资料中的党派或其他标志旁边，比如西瓜表情符号，象征着在加沙战争中与巴勒斯坦人的团结。其他人正在与人工智能开发者约会的道德问题进行斗争，考虑行业合作伙伴可以带来的经济利益，权衡是否在不确定的未来生孩子，甚至将自己的爱情生活完全交给人工智能。

在伯克利附近的一条街上，我遇到了凯尔。 （他的名字已被更改，以便他可以公开谈论他的个人生活。）凯尔是人工智能安全非营利组织的研究员，尽管他才 20 岁出头，但他已经在考虑死亡了。在人工智能安全领域，一些专家认为，由于人工智能的接管，人类有 10% 的机会灭绝。当他与潜在伴侣进行对话时，这种世界末日的可能性始终是他的首要考虑：人工智能的快速发展决定了他如何思考是否想要孩子，或者他可能长期居住在哪里——如果有长期的话。

“很难进行规划对话，因为我并不真正期望有长期的未来。”

“很多人都在规划自己想要的 5 年、10 年、15 年后的生活，”凯尔说道，抬起目光，眺望远方。他告诉我，生活可能会发生变化，这取决于世界是否能够正确调整人工智能。 “对我来说，很难进行规划对话，因为我真的不期望有长期的未来，”他说。他尝试亲自进行这些对话，而不是通过短信进行，这样约会对象就可以提出后续问题，了解他为何以这种方式看待未来。

目前，他专注于寻找一个他喜欢共度时光的伴侣。

当我问凯尔是否愿意与从事人工智能或科技工作的人约会时，他说他必须认真考虑一下。他认为，很多在前沿人工智能公司工作的人都在做他认为非常令人发指的事情。 “他们并没有认真考虑自己的行为的社会影响，因为他们主要是为了薪水或者因为这很有趣，”他说。

但布莱恩在一家前沿人工智能公司工作，也要求使用化名，他认为在浪漫方面，对人工智能的感受并不重要。

“我只是认为这根本不是一个因素。就像，这是最不相关的事情，”最近开始恋爱的布莱恩说。对他来说，约会更多的是权衡一系列因素：某人如何谈论和解决问题，他们如何享受乐趣。尽管他的日常工作（无论像凯尔这样的人可能会如何看待他），他相信更多的锻炼和更好的外表可能比任何人工智能或非人工智能附属机构更能增加某人获得比赛的机会。但是，他说，“它相互作用的一种方式是，有一群人因人工智能而变得富有，而且，你知道，富有总是有好处的。”

items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Perplexity is launching "Teammates," always-on agents that work through ongoing projects on their own virtual machines. The feature requires the Max plan at $200 per month, well above similar offerings from OpenAI or Anthropic. The market for always-on agents is getting crowded.

items.title: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails
items.title_en: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
Another email with a similar pitch (adding call transcripts to the list of desired information) raised the stakes to a possible $2 million. “Public data is exhausted, and the labs are spending over $45B on private data to build better models,” writes someone named Cora.

While I was aware that AI companies are buying expert data from various sources, there hasn’t been that much attention paid to it. But once I looked into it, I discovered that this business is way bigger than I suspected—and according to its practitioners, it could have as much impact on workers and society as the data centers that are dominating the news these days.

The companies that contacted me are part of an industry boom in data acquisition that’s been quietly buying the workflows of sizable companies and is still so hungry that it’s bleeding into our inboxes. A freelance writer recently wrote about her experience with a company called Handshake, which offered her $1,000 for her work on a single story. (She didn’t sell.) A representative from Handshake confirmed the offer to me: “We license professional documents across a lot of fields so the labs can test and train how models handle real knowledge work,” he said. “Journalism is one of those fields.” Handshake tells me that a big part of its business is buying graduate students’ papers and coursework.

An entrepreneur friend of mine tells me he’s been getting mail from multiple companies whose business is “helping startups wind down their companies," as one email from a company named Sunset explained it. “We handle the full process, scrubbing and anonymizing the data so the company people and any identifying details are stripped out, then brokering the deal with the labs.”

Those newer data acquisition startups are hoping to achieve the quick success of the dominant companies in the field, which themselves are only a few years old. Industry leaders Handshake, Micro1, and Mercor are snapping up databases as if it were a modern gold rush. The industry leader seems to be Mercor, founded in 2023; last year its three cofounders became billionaires at 22. Like all the companies, it claims to have partnerships with just about all the major AI labs. (The response from the companies themselves was more circumspect: Anthropic acknowledges that there’s a big market for data, but told me that it doesn’t buy workflow from live companies like WIRED. OpenAI didn’t come up with a response before publication.)

In an interview, Mercor CEO Brendan Foody told me that the market is poised to explode as the AI industry seeks dramatically more data. Mercor originally started as an AI recruiting company, but as the team got to know the players, it learned that the big labs were frustrated by the quality of the data. Generally, the industry had been hiring experts to simulate actual workflow, but that didn’t capture the messiness of an actual operating business. He urged me to consider that Big AI has two bottomless needs: compute and data. While the industry is very publicly making giant investments in the former, data gathering is just as important.

Foody is ready when I bring up privacy concerns. When a business streams the data to Mercor, the company strips out any personal identifying information, or PII. This de-identification can be verified, he says. Like all the people in data acquisition I spoke to, he felt that technology has solved the privacy issues of buying all that information.

Not surprisingly, Micro1 CEO Ali Ansari agrees that the data-buying market will soon approach that of AI’s compute infrastructure. He says that today, labs, enterprises, and robotics companies pay about $40 to $50 billion a year to get data. (I was unable to verify this.) “In the next two to four years, this is going to be over a trillion dollars a year,” says Ansari, who founded the company in 2022. Micro1 uses the information it buys largely to improve AI models it builds itself, but it also sells to big AI firms.

“Pretty much everybody’s trying to get into the data space now because there’s so much demand,” he says. “If you look at the YC startups, about half of them are data companies.” (Actually, it’s more—in the most recent YC batch, 40 of the 65 launched companies are classified as data startups.)

The Wild West aspect to this quest for fresh data got rare exposure when a bankrupt Spirit Airlines put its digital assets up for sale. The corpus included 80,000 email accounts, 500 million internal messages, 20.6 million Microsoft Sharepoint files, and a million time-card records. Google seemingly got the prize with a $10 million bid, but then Micro1 topped it by $2.5 million, setting off an argument over who the winner was. Presently the sale is on hold, for a reason that calls into question the entire practice of selling off human workflow: The flight attendants’ union has charged that the sale involved their private information.

The union’s objections cast a light on the dark side of this gold rush. Despite the claims of virtually all the data companies that no PII goes into AI models, critics feel that there is still danger of personal data leaking out. “It’s not clear that anonymizing can fully get rid of privacy issues,” says Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, general counsel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, which has filed an amicus brief on behalf of the flight attendants. “Emails and Teams messages contain unstructured data, which is harder to root out. There may be messages where employees talk about doctor’s appointments or family issues.”

“We haven't set the norms and the standards for data acquisition, and it’s not being done appropriately ” says Gordon Ritter, a venture capitalist who has taken on the issue as a cause. “The AI industry is moving far faster than our ability to actually set the standards, and it's partially intentional.”

Probably the most troubling aspect of the data-gathering movement is that, in essence, it enlists workers, not always with explicit consent, to contribute to an effort where the ultimate goal is to replace or automate the human work that goes into all those documents, messages, and emails. When Mercor says that its motto is “Organizing human intelligence to power the AI economy,” the unspoken message is that the economy of flesh and blood workers will have less work to do. As the president of the flight attendant’s union told an interviewer: “This is really only data that became valuable in the age of AI in order to train models to replace jobs and commodify other portions of working in a work environment.”

When I ask Micro1’s Ansari whether one day the default for corporations will be selling their workflow data to big AI companies on an ongoing basis, he answers affirmatively. “I think it’s going to become more common than ads as a revenue line item for companies,” he says. I note that there is already considerable pushback to AI, and that people might not be happy with the idea that everything they do at work gets funneled into the maw of a big AI model.

“I think it’s a fair point,” says Ansari. But, in his view, such objections will be manageable. He suggests that workers will understand that the fruits of their labor will result in better AI models, which will make their lives easier. “You have to think of the upside, the abundance that AI can result in.” (I’ve found that the future abundance that AI will supposedly produce is a handy justification for all sorts of compromises.)

I did follow up on one of the cold pitches I got, from a woman whose email domain was gorexen.com. A “gorexen,” by the way, is a fusion of two Pokemon critters that “siphons the body fluids of prey through its thin, tubular mouth.” She set up a meeting with me with a two-year-old company called Tenkara (the name seems to be associated with a type of Japanese fly fishing). I found myself talking to “head of commercialization” Jonah Stillman, a young startup-looking dude sitting in an office in San Francisco.

I began peppering him with questions. Tenkara’s quest for data seems to be to boost the quality of its AI model to run office operations for manufacturing companies. (How WIRED’s archives would help is a mystery.) He confirmed that a big part of his job is doing calls like this to snap up data. I told him that the set of our meeting gave me a Glengarry Glen Ross vibe, but he wasn’t familiar with the reference.

I am, of course, not authorized to sell the documentation of WIRED’s editorial process to an AI company, and I did not risk my job by offering Jonah and his company the goods. I also wouldn’t be too pleased if my bosses made the sale.
